title: General Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given a linear recurrence sequence with rational coefficients and rational initial values, decide whether any term of the sequence is zero. A decision procedure must terminate on every input, rather than merely enumerating zero terms or handling restricted spectral configurations.
status: The problem originates in twentieth-century work surrounding the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem. Substantial conditional decidability results exist — see Bilu et al. (2022), *Skolem Meets Schanuel*, arXiv:2204.13417, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2022.20, and Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328 — but unconditional general decidability remains unresolved.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that, on every rational linear recurrence sequence, halts and correctly decides whether some term equals zero.
why: It settles a fundamental obstruction to exact reachability analysis for linear programs.
key_works: Bilu et al. (2022), *Skolem Meets Schanuel*, arXiv:2204.13417, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2022.20; Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328.
aliases: Zero-occurrence problem for linear recurrence sequences.

title: Skolem problem at order five
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given an arbitrary rational linear recurrence sequence of order five, is there an algorithm that decides whether zero occurs in the sequence? The crux lies in simple recurrences whose characteristic roots include two dominant complex-conjugate pairs of equal modulus together with a smaller real root.
status: The Skolem problem is decidable for orders at most four. Many specific order-five configurations have been settled, but the complete order-five problem remains open according to the 2026 survey (Bacik et al., 2026, *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*; see also Lipton et al., 2022, *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328).
solved_when: A decision procedure is exhibited that, for every rational linear recurrence sequence of order five, correctly determines whether some term equals zero.
why: It would cross the first genuinely open dimensional boundary of the Skolem problem rather than attacking the unrestricted general case, which remains out of reach.
key_works: Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328; Bacik et al. (2026), *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*.

title: Bounded continuous Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given a rational linear differential system, a rational observation vector, and a bounded rational time interval, decide whether the observed trajectory is exactly zero anywhere in that interval. Formally, this asks for an algorithm deciding the existence of a real t in the interval with the observation functional vanishing at t.
status: Unconditional decidability is unresolved in general. Conditional procedures and substantial special cases exist, building on Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (2015/2016), *On the Skolem Problem for Continuous Linear Dynamical Systems* (arXiv:1506.00695); the problem is connected to Schanuel-type transcendence conjectures in number theory and to exact zero detection in computable analysis.
solved_when: An unconditional decision procedure is given for arbitrary rational linear differential systems, rational observation vectors, and bounded rational time intervals.
why: It is the exact event-detection problem for linear continuous-system verification: numerical approximation cannot certify exact tangential zeros, so a decision procedure is needed to verify such events.
key_works: Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (2015/2016), *On the Skolem Problem for Continuous Linear Dynamical Systems*, arXiv:1506.00695.

title: Unbounded continuous Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given a linear differential system and a linear observation of its state, decide whether the observed output ever equals zero at some nonnegative real time, with no finite time horizon imposed. Equivalently, decide whether there exists t ≥ 0 with y(t) = 0 for the observed trajectory, in the unbounded-time setting.
status: Restricted frequency configurations of the problem admit reductions or algorithms, notably in work by Bell, Delvenne, Jungers, and Blondel (2010), *The Continuous Skolem-Pisot Problem* (arXiv:0809.2189), and Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (arXiv:1506.00695). The unrestricted problem remains open and tied to difficult effective Diophantine-approximation questions in number theory, specifically the computability of Diophantine approximation types.
solved_when: An algorithm (or a conclusive decidability proof, positive or negative) is obtained for the general, unrestricted unbounded-time continuous Skolem problem — that is, for arbitrary linear differential systems and observations, with no restrictions on the system's exponential-polynomial frequency configuration.
why: A decision procedure here directly supports unbounded-time reachability and safety verification for linear continuous-time plants, where finite-horizon analyses are not enough.
key_works: Bell, Delvenne, Jungers, and Blondel (2010), *The Continuous Skolem-Pisot Problem*, arXiv:0809.2189; Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell, arXiv:1506.00695.

title: Numerically reliable stochastic-game stopping criteria
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Can we build stochastic-game solvers whose output is exact or comes with a certified interval, so that termination is announced with a sound certificate even when values are nearly tied and floating-point roundoff is in play? The goal is a solver whose "converged" verdict is itself a checkable guarantee rather than a numerical impression.
status: Sound value-iteration approaches exist (Quatmann and Katoen, 2018, *Sound Value Iteration*; tooling in Dehnert et al. 2017, *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311). The remaining gap is a single approach combining large instances, tight error guarantees, independently checked certificates, and predictable termination behavior.
solved_when: A solver exists that handles large instances while providing tight error guarantees, produces termination certificates that can be independently checked, and exhibits predictable termination behavior, remaining sound near value ties and under floating-point roundoff.
why: It prevents apparently converged numerical values from silently becoming unsound verification results, so that quantitative guarantees about stochastic games can be trusted as delivered rather than re-derived.
key_works: Quatmann and Katoen (2018), *Sound Value Iteration*; Dehnert et al. (2017), *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311.

title: Exact complexity of three-dimensional VASS reachability
open: What is the exact complexity of the reachability problem for three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Formally, the goal is to close the gap between the known PSPACE lower bound and the current 2EXPSPACE upper bound for 3-VASS reachability.
status: A 2025 result proves an elementary upper bound of 2EXPSPACE membership, against known PSPACE hardness, so the question "Is 3-VASS reachability elementary?" is no longer open (Czerwiński, Jecker, Lasota, and Orlikowski (2025), *Reachability in 3-VASS Is Elementary*, arXiv:2502.13916, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.153). The remaining question is the exact complexity within that range.
solved_when: The gap is closed by matching upper and lower bounds — i.e., a proof that 3-VASS reachability is in PSPACE (matching the PSPACE hardness) or a hardness proof raising the lower bound to 2EXPSPACE.
why: A tight bound would locate a sharp low-dimensional boundary in counter-system verification, pinning down where dimension three sits between tractability and intractability.
key_works: Czerwiński, Jecker, Lasota, and Orlikowski (2025), *Reachability in 3-VASS Is Elementary*, arXiv:2502.13916, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.153.

title: Incremental SMT certificates with sound scope management
open: How should proof logs for incremental SMT solving be designed so that they stay compact yet remain sound across push/pop scopes, assumptions, preprocessing steps, and shared learned lemmas? In other words, what certificate structure lets a checker verify each step using only the declarations and assumptions actually in scope at the time it was derived?
status: General proof formats and checkers for SMT already exist (e.g., Alethe, *Towards a Generic SMT Proof Format*, 2021, HAL:hal-03341413; Andreotti et al. 2023, *Carcara*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-30823-9_19), but none yet provides reliable cross-session reuse without accepting lemmas outside the assumptions that justify them.
solved_when: A proof-log format and checker exist that support incremental solving with push/pop, assumptions, preprocessing, and shared learned lemmas, and reliably support cross-session reuse of verification work without ever accepting a lemma outside the assumptions that justify it.
why: It enables caching of verification work across sessions without risking stale-proof unsoundness — the certificate analogue of sound dependency tracking and cache invalidation in build systems.
key_works: *Alethe: Towards a Generic SMT Proof Format* (2021), HAL:hal-03341413; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-30823-9_19.

title: Superpolynomial Frege lower bounds
open: Is there an explicit family of propositional tautologies that no general Frege system can prove with only polynomially many proof lines? Formally, exhibit a tautology family requiring superpolynomial-size proofs in unrestricted Frege systems.
status: A longstanding central problem in proof complexity. Strong lower bounds are known for weaker systems, but they do not extend automatically to unrestricted Frege; see Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*, EMS chapter, and Beame and Pitassi, *Propositional Proof Complexity: Past, Present, and Future*.
solved_when: An explicit tautology family is exhibited for which every Frege proof has superpolynomial size.
why: A solution would expose the intrinsic limitations of powerful propositional proof engines and mark a decisive separation within proof complexity.
key_works: Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*, EMS chapter; Beame and Pitassi, *Propositional Proof Complexity: Past, Present, and Future*.

title: Automated liveness proofs for fine-grained concurrent libraries
open: Can we automatically infer and machine-check termination and progress arguments for substantial fine-grained concurrent libraries, both lock-free and blocking, with only minimal manual obligation engineering?
status: TaDA Live (D’Osualdo, Farzan, Gardner, and Sutherland, 2021, *TaDA Live: Compositional Reasoning for Termination of Fine-Grained Concurrent Programs*, arXiv:1901.05750, DOI:10.1145/3477082) establishes compositional reasoning for fine-grained termination; automation at production-library scale remains a separate, unsolved challenge.
solved_when: A tool infers and verifies liveness proofs for a substantial, production-scale lock-free or blocking concurrent library, with the residual manual proof obligations kept to a minimum rather than hand-engineered per library.
why: It pushes automated verification of concurrent code beyond memory safety and partial correctness to actual progress, the property clients of concurrent libraries ultimately depend on.
key_works: D’Osualdo, Farzan, Gardner, and Sutherland (2021), *TaDA Live: Compositional Reasoning for Termination of Fine-Grained Concurrent Programs*, arXiv:1901.05750, DOI:10.1145/3477082.

title: C provenance semantics aligned across standard, compiler, and verifier
open: Can the C community converge on a single, maintained provenance model whose permitted behaviors agree across the language specification, optimizing compilers, and verification tools for a declared fragment of C?
status: Cerberus and related provenance proposals (Memarian et al. 2019, *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Memarian 2023, *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981) substantially clarify the problem, but complete agreement across the toolchain remains an integration target.
solved_when: A maintained provenance semantics exists and its permitted behaviors demonstrably agree across language specifications, compilers, and verification tools for the declared C fragment.
why: Without alignment, pointer–integer conversions and object identity receive contradictory interpretations across the toolchain, breaking portability and trust in verified low-level code.
key_works: Memarian et al. (2019), *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Memarian (2023), *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981.

title: Mechanized cross-language undefined-behavior boundaries
open: When can programs written under different undefined-behavior conventions be safely linked, so that each component retains the guarantees its own language promised? The goal is a mechanized semantic account giving provable conditions under which cross-language composition of components with differing undefined-behavior rules preserves each component’s guarantees.
status: C provenance and Rust unsafe-code foundations expose the relevant differences between languages’ undefined-behavior rules; language-local correctness has been shown to be insufficient. Key works: Memarian et al. (2019), *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*.
solved_when: A mechanized specification and machine-checked proof exist that characterize linking conditions under which components with different undefined-behavior rules preserve each component’s guarantees, demonstrated across languages with genuinely differing UB conventions (e.g., C provenance and Rust unsafe code).
why: It would support verified mixed C, Rust, assembly, and managed-language systems, where correctness proved within any single language is insufficient.
key_works: Memarian et al. (2019), *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*.

title: Full processor refinement to executable ISA semantics
open: Can a substantial out-of-order processor implementation be proven, end to end, to refine its architectural model? Formally, the goal is a full refinement proof covering speculation, exceptions, interrupts, and memory ordering.
status: The foundations are in place: Sail ISA models (Armstrong et al. 2019, DOI:10.1145/3290384) give executable semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS, and parametric hardware-verification frameworks such as Kami (Choi et al. 2017, DOI:10.1145/3110268) support building verified hardware. However, a full implementation-level proof remains specific to a single processor and its feature envelope; no general full refinement result exists.
solved_when: A refinement proof is carried from a real out-of-order processor implementation to its architectural (ISA) semantics, covering speculation, exceptions, interrupts, and memory ordering — with no feature left outside the verified envelope.
why: It is the missing link that would let software proofs carry down to the hardware actually executing them, closing the gap between verified programs and verified machines.
key_works: Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS*, DOI:10.1145/3290384; Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268.

title: Verified vectorized cryptography across architectures
open: Can cryptographic code be both fully verified and as fast as the best hand-tuned vectorized implementations? Concretely, produce high-performance vectorized implementations whose machine-checked proofs cover instruction semantics, lane operations, alignment, and fallback dispatch.
status: EverCrypt (Protzenko et al., 2020) verifies cross-platform cryptographic components and dispatch mechanisms, but broad architecture and algorithm coverage remains a continuing target. Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics* (DOI:10.1145/3290384), provide foundational instruction-set semantics that such verification efforts build on.
solved_when: A verified vectorized cryptographic implementation exists whose proofs cover instruction semantics, lane operations, alignment, and fallback dispatch, while achieving high performance across architectures without unacceptable performance loss relative to unverified vectorized code.
why: It removes the current trade-off where formal assurance forces an unacceptable performance sacrifice, so security-critical systems can adopt verified cryptography without giving up the speed of vectorized, hardware-accelerated implementations.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

title: End-to-end finite-precision differential privacy
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can we prove differential privacy for a mechanism as it actually executes, with floating-point sampling, clipping, rounding, exceptional values, and observable failures all included in the analysis, rather than for an idealized real-number abstraction of it?
status: Mathematical privacy proofs and finite-precision verification currently exist separately; connecting them end-to-end remains open and is viewed as essential. Key works include Barthe et al. (2016), arXiv:1601.05047, and Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, arXiv:1707.02115.
solved_when: A verification exists that connects the mathematical privacy proof of a mechanism to a finite-precision analysis of its executable form, covering floating-point sampling, clipping, rounding, exceptional values, and observable failures, so the end-to-end guarantee holds of the running implementation.
why: Without it, ideal-real-number proofs can hide leakage that the implementation actually exhibits, so systems believed private in theory may not be private as deployed.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), arXiv:1601.05047; Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Scalable certified floating-point error analysis with branches
open: Can we compute tight end-to-end error bounds for floating-point programs in which rounding errors can alter control flow, including for inputs whose exact values lie near branch boundaries?
status: FloVer verifies numerical error certificates, but unstable tests and discrete choices introduce additional analysis challenges; the key works are Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115, and Lohar, Darulova, Putot, and Goubault (2018), *Discrete Choice in the Presence of Numerical Uncertainties*.
solved_when: A scalable, certified analysis yields tight end-to-end error bounds covering unstable branch tests and discrete choices, including behavior on paths near branch boundaries.
why: It prevents small arithmetic errors from triggering large behavioral changes, which is the dominant failure mode of discontinuous numerical algorithms.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Lohar, Darulova, Putot, and Goubault (2018), *Discrete Choice in the Presence of Numerical Uncertainties*.

title: Automatic discovery of nonlinear differential invariants
open: Can a tool automatically find useful nonlinear differential invariants for hybrid systems and discharge the resulting safety proofs with independently checked certificates, even for difficult parameterized systems?
status: Differential dynamic logic and KeYmaera X (Platzer 2016, DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; Fulton et al. 2015) provide a mature proof foundation, but invariant discovery remains a major automation burden.
solved_when: A method exists that automatically discovers nonlinear differential invariants and produces proofs that are independently verified by a trusted proof kernel, handling difficult parameterized systems.
why: It removes the dominant manual mathematical effort in hybrid-system safety proofs, making verified safety analysis of nonlinear dynamics practical at scale.
key_works: Platzer (2016), *A Complete Uniform Substitution Calculus for Differential Dynamic Logic*, DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

title: Complete mediation of agent side effects
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can an agent execution environment be built so that every externally visible action — including those of subprocesses, delegated agents, plugins, and direct network access — provably passes through a policy-enforcing boundary?
status: AgentSpec (Wang, Poskitt, and Sun, 2025, *AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents*, arXiv:2503.18666) demonstrates customizable runtime enforcement, but complete mediation across a realistic execution environment remains a stronger target. Related work in security engineering studies tamper-resistant reference monitors.
solved_when: A realistic execution environment exists with a complete-mediation guarantee covering subprocesses, delegated agents, plugins, and direct network access, so no externally visible agent action can bypass the policy boundary.
why: It makes safety independent of whether the language model follows its instructions: even a misbehaving or prompt-injected model cannot cause effects the policy forbids.
key_works: Wang, Poskitt, and Sun (2025), *AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents*, arXiv:2503.18666.

title: Complete machine-checked metatheory for Lean’s implemented kernel
open: Can the correctness of Lean's implemented type checker be fully verified in a machine, relative to an explicit formal account of its logic and conversion behavior? why: It would remove reliance on informal arguments about the trusted kernel of a widely used proof assistant, whose soundness underpins every Lean formalization.

title: Human-useful explanations of failed proof search
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: When an automated proof search fails, can a system explain the failure to a human in a way that is faithful to what the search actually did — identifying which lemma was missing, which assumptions conflicted, or why the chosen induction principle was unsuitable?
status: Instrumentation and proof-analysis tools — e.g., work drawing on REPLICA-style REPL instrumentation for Coq (Ringer et al., 2020) and the survey QED at Large (Ringer et al., 2019) — already expose detailed proof-search traces, but converting those traces into useful, nonfabricated explanations remains an open target.
solved_when: A system produces explanations of failed proof searches that identify missing lemmas, incompatible assumptions, or unsuitable induction principles, and these explanations are validated against the actual recorded search behavior rather than fabricated after the fact.
why: It turns proof automation from an opaque oracle into a collaborative partner, letting a human diagnose and repair the obstacles the automation actually encountered.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2020), *REPLICA: REPL Instrumentation for Coq Analysis*; Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*.

title: Tenfold cheaper whole-program safety analysis
open: Can sound whole-program static analysis be made ten times cheaper without giving up its guarantees — that is, can total analysis cost be cut by at least an order of magnitude on a frozen multi-language corpus while preserving a declared soundness envelope and false-alarm rate?
status: This is a proposed benchmarked moonshot; no solution yet exists. Comparisons are required to include annotation labor, memory, and incremental reruns rather than solver time alone. solved_when: A 10× or greater reduction in total analysis cost is demonstrated on a frozen multi-language corpus, with soundness envelope and false-alarm rate preserved, and where the measured cost accounts for annotation labor, memory, and incremental reruns rather than solver time alone.
why: It would make sound analysis practical for development workflows that currently cannot afford it, enabling cost-effective defect prevention at scale.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977); Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Polynomial-time parity games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Can arbitrary finite parity games be solved in polynomial time — or is there a complexity-theoretic reason no such algorithm exists?

solved_when: A rigorously validated polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary finite parity games is accepted, or an appropriate complexity-theoretic obstruction to polynomial-time solvability is established.
why: It would strengthen a central algorithmic foundation of reactive synthesis and temporal-logic verification, where parity-game solving is the core computational step.

title: Polynomial-time mean-payoff games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm to decide the winner of a finite two-player mean-payoff game? Formally, can the winner be determined in time polynomial in the number of vertices and edges and in the bit-length of the edge weights?

solved_when: A deterministic or randomized algorithm decides the winner (equivalently, computes the values) of any finite mean-payoff game in time polynomial in the graph size and the binary encoding length of the weights.
why: A polynomial-time algorithm would place mean-payoff games in P and make automated synthesis for controllers and reactive systems with long-run resource, energy, and performance objectives practical at scale.

title: Word equations with linear length constraints
open: Is satisfiability decidable for word equations over a finite alphabet when they are combined with linear constraints on the lengths of the strings? In other words, does the satisfiability problem remain decidable once linear arithmetic over length variables is added to word equations?

title: Cutoffs for dynamically changing populations
open: When the set of participants in a distributed protocol can grow, shrink, or change roles during a run, when can we still verify it once and for all? why: It would let correctness proofs survive autoscaling and membership churn, so a verified protocol remains trustworthy as its population changes rather than being tied to a fixed set of processes.

title: Exact parameter regions for realistic timed models

title: Robustness-preserving timed abstraction

title: Unbounded recursive-concurrent verification beyond fixed context bounds
open: Which classes of recursive concurrent programs can be verified compositionally, with a procedure that terminates, without fixing a global bound on thread context switches? More precisely, the goal is to delimit program classes that admit such compositional, terminating verification in the unbounded-concurrency setting.
status: Thread-modular analyses and compositional logics give partial answers; relevant work includes *Effect Summaries for Thread-Modular Analysis* (2017, arXiv:1705.03701) and Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*. The target is an expressive decidable or effectively checkable fragment, not decidability for unrestricted concurrent programs.
solved_when: A useful program class is identified together with a compositional verification procedure that terminates on that class while reasoning about unboundedly many thread interleavings — no global context-switch bound in the analysis.
why: It separates a genuine unbounded-concurrency guarantee from what bounded exploration actually proves, giving verified programs a guarantee that does not silently expire as thread counts or interleavings grow.
key_works: *Effect Summaries for Thread-Modular Analysis* (2017), arXiv:1705.03701; Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.

why: It turns failed liveness proofs into actionable diagnostics rather than dead ends, giving users concrete evidence of where and why the liveness property breaks.

title: Complete termination criteria for Nielsen-based string solving
open: For which residual classes of word equations does the Nielsen transformation procedure provably terminate once length constraints are propagated into the reasoning — going beyond the cut-graph criteria already established? why: It converts heuristic string solvers into procedures with explicit termination envelopes, so SMT solvers handling strings with length constraints can guarantee termination rather than relying on incomplete heuristics.

title: Complete SMT proof coverage without trusted solver escape hatches
open: Can every successful answer from a widely used SMT fragment be exported as a proof that a small, independently maintained checker will accept — including all preprocessing steps? title: Stable quantified SMT reasoning for evolving specifications
open: Can we build SMT-based quantifier-instantiation and proof-repair methods whose success survives semantics-preserving edits — declaration reordering, harmless auxiliary lemmas, renaming — so that a proof that closes today still closes after routine refactoring? Formally, the goal is reasoning techniques whose behavior is stable under meaning-preserving mutations of the specification.
status: SMT-backed verification is effective, but solver sensitivity to such changes is a documented proof-engineering concern (Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045; Why3 project, maintained verification-platform documentation).
solved_when: Quantifier-instantiation and proof-repair methods exist whose verification success is demonstrably robust to semantics-preserving changes (declaration reordering, auxiliary lemmas, renaming), as evidenced by longitudinal mutation testing rather than a single benchmark score.
why: Without such robustness, verification pipelines become brittle under ordinary development, so proofs that once closed silently break after benign edits and engineers lose trust in automated verification.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045; Why3 project, maintained verification-platform documentation.

title: Scalable mixed floating-point and bit-vector certificates

solved_when: A certificate-checking pipeline exists that composes bit-level encodings with numerical certificate checkers efficiently, so that large mixed floating-point, bit-vector, and memory queries can be certified at scale with no unverifiable trusted components and no blowup to enormous bit-blasted proofs.
why: It would give trustworthy verification of low-level numerical software and hardware, where floating-point and bit-level reasoning must interoperate.

title: General algebraic proof-system lower bounds
open: Can we prove superpolynomial lower bounds for explicit instances in powerful algebraic proof systems whose certificates are represented by unrestricted arithmetic circuits? why: It would clarify whether algebraic certificates can evade the bottlenecks that block conventional propositional proof-complexity lower bounds, connecting proof complexity to the arithmetic-circuit frontier.

why: It makes large parallel verification workloads independently trustworthy, so results from distributed solving can be checked rather than taken on faith.

open: Can we shrink the certificates that SAT and SMT solvers store so that a preregistered suite of large instances needs at least a hundred times less space, without expanding what a checker must trust and without making the cost of reconstructing and verifying the proof impractical?

title: Proof-carrying solver portfolios
open: Can a solver portfolio that orchestrates SAT solving, SMT solving, abstract interpretation, and numerical reasoning export a single machine-checked argument that covers every assumption made across engines, including the cross-engine ones?
status: Individual certificate systems exist (e.g., foundational proof certificates per Chihani, Miller, and Renaud, and the Carcara system of Andreotti et al., 2023), but trusting each solver independently does not establish the soundness of their orchestration; the compositional case remains open.
solved_when: A portfolio combining SAT, SMT, abstract interpretation, and numerical reasoning exists that exports one checked certificate covering all cross-engine assumptions, so that no individual solver must be independently trusted for the orchestration to be sound.
why: It would enable heterogeneous automation without a correspondingly large trusted base, replacing per-solver trust with one verified argument for the whole orchestration.

title: Automatically synthesized abstract domains with checked soundness
open: Can a system automatically construct an abstract domain, together with its transfer functions, that is tailored to a given analysis problem — and justify its own correctness? Formally, the goal is automated domain synthesis producing machine-checked soundness proofs and measured precision/cost trade-offs that remain useful as real programs change.
status: Abstract interpretation supplies the foundational framework, rooted in Cousot and Cousot (1977), *Abstract Interpretation: A Unified Lattice Model for Static Analysis of Programs by Construction or Approximation of Fixpoints*, DOI:10.1145/512950.512973; the open target is automated domain construction that stays useful on changing real programs, with related directions in machine learning of symbolic representations with guarantees.
solved_when: A system exists that, for a given target program or program family, synthesizes an abstract domain and transfer functions automatically, ships with machine-checked soundness proofs, and demonstrates quantified precision-versus-cost trade-offs on changing real programs.
why: Today, building an effective static analysis requires an expert to hand-design domains; automating that step would make sound static analysis accessible without domain-design expertise.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977), *Abstract Interpretation: A Unified Lattice Model for Static Analysis of Programs by Construction or Approximation of Fixpoints*, DOI:10.1145/512950.512973.

title: Predictably precise widening
open: Can we construct widening strategies for abstract interpretation that come with explicit, checkable explanations of precision loss and whose behavior is robust under equivalent transformations of the program being analyzed?
status: Widening resolves convergence problems in abstract interpretation but introduces analysis-dependent approximation; no universal optimality is assumed. The goal is predictable behavior on declared domain families, per Cousot and Cousot (1977), DOI:10.1145/512950.512973, and Cousot, *Abstract Interpretation in a Nutshell*.
solved_when: A widening strategy is given whose precision-loss behavior is explicitly explained and checkable, and which behaves predictably (equivalently) on declared domain families under equivalent program transformations.
why: It would make false alarms from static analyses understandable to users and make analysis results stable across semantically equivalent program forms, rather than varying arbitrarily with representation.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977), DOI:10.1145/512950.512973; Cousot, *Abstract Interpretation in a Nutshell*.

title: Certified relational heap-and-numerical analysis
open: Can a single static analyzer jointly track heap shape, aliasing, arithmetic invariants, and concurrency permissions, with the domain reductions in the combined analyzer formally proved sound?
status: Shape analyses, numerical domains, and separation logics each provide strong components, as in Cousot and Cousot (1977) and Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; their scalable, automatically tuned combination remains an engineering frontier.
solved_when: A working analyzer exists that combines heap shape, aliasing, arithmetic relationships, and concurrency permissions, and every reduction between its domains carries a formal soundness proof.
why: It targets bug classes — such as those in concurrent mutable-graph algorithms — that vanish from view when heap and arithmetic facts are analyzed separately.

title: Reusable IC3 invariants across program revisions
open: When a verified program is revised, can its property-directed reachability (IC3/PDR) proof clauses be carried over to the new revision — with a sound account of exactly which clauses remain inductively valid, and an efficient repair procedure for those invalidated by the change?
status: IC3/PDR is established as an effective form of incremental inductive reasoning, as in Bradley (2012), *Understanding IC3*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-31612-8_1; however, cross-revision proof reuse demands stronger dependency management than ordinary within-run incrementality, and related work on change impact (Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*) has not closed this gap.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a program and its IC3 invariant clauses plus a code revision, soundly determines which clauses remain valid, repairs invalidated dependencies, and re-establishes the full inductive invariant at lower verification cost than re-running IC3 from scratch; no quantitative targets are stated, so this natural correctness-plus-efficiency criterion applies.
why: Continuous verification of evolving code currently pays the full cost of re-proving after every change; reusable invariants would cut that recurring cost in industrial verification loops.
key_works: Bradley (2012), *Understanding IC3*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-31612-8_1; Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Explainable failed invariant generalization
open: Can a model checker, when a candidate invariant fails, explain *why* it failed — telling the developer whether the failure stems from genuinely missing state, from imprecision in the abstraction, or from insufficient inductive strength?
status: IC3 and related methods generate and refine inductive clauses, but no such diagnostic interface exists today; the proposed target is a validated diagnostic interface rather than another opaque heuristic (Bradley 2012, *Understanding IC3*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-31612-8_1).
solved_when: A validated diagnostic interface exists that, on invariant failure, classifies the cause as missing state, abstraction imprecision, or insufficient induction strength, and this classification is validated rather than an opaque heuristic.
why: It lets developers repair specifications and abstractions directly instead of blindly tuning solvers.

title: Compositional verification of data-dependent resource bounds

solved_when: A compositional method exists that infers and certifies data-dependent time, allocation, and energy bounds for programs combining recursion, mutable structures, and input-dependent control flow, with all hardware and cost-model assumptions made explicit.
why: It extends formal guarantees from "does not crash" to operational feasibility, allowing resource behavior itself to become a verified property of the program.

title: Confidence-aware analysis without weakening soundness claims
open: Can a static analysis be made confidence-aware — reporting statistical confidence alongside its findings — while keeping a strict separation between what is proved universally sound, what is claimed probabilistically under an assumed distribution, and what is merely a heuristic ranking of alarms?

why: It prevents probabilistic alarm prioritization from being mislabeled as universal verification, so downstream users of the analysis know exactly which guarantees they actually hold.

title: Minimal nonvacuous environment assumptions
open: Can we automatically infer environment assumptions under which a given specification becomes realizable, while guaranteeing that the inferred assumptions do not rule out the intended deployment or render the guarantee trivial? In other words, is there a principled notion of minimality for environment assumptions that synthesis tools can compute and users can trust?
status: Assumption engineering is recognized as fundamental to synthesis, but the target still requires explicit minimality criteria and independently reviewed environment relevance; no such framework is in place. solved_when: A method exists that, given a specification, produces environment assumptions making it realizable, together with explicit minimality criteria satisfied by those assumptions and a means of independently establishing their relevance to the intended environment.
why: It prevents synthesizing controllers that are formally correct only for impossible or irrelevant worlds, which is the central practical failure mode of assumption-driven synthesis.

why: It would let synthesis take part in ordinary iterative development, where requirements evolve constantly and full re-synthesis with re-verification is too disruptive and costly.

title: Scalable alternating-quantifier hyperproperty checking
open: Can we build a checker that verifies properties involving alternating quantification over executions of a realistic system, without ever materializing the self-product that naive hyperproperty checking requires? why: Security and refinement statements typically compare multiple possible executions of the same system; a scalable method for these makes such properties, which are exactly the ones that matter in practice, verifiable rather than aspirational.

title: Certified almost-sure termination for nonlinear probabilistic loops
open: Can we automatically synthesize machine-checkable almost-sure termination arguments for useful nonlinear probabilistic programs with unbounded state? That is, produce — without human proof effort — a certificate, checkable by a proof assistant, that such a program terminates with probability one.
status: Martingales, expectation invariants, and specialized analyses provide partial methods for proving almost-sure termination; universal completeness is not claimed.
solved_when: A tool exists that, given useful nonlinear probabilistic loops with unbounded state, automatically synthesizes termination arguments that are machine-checkable and establish almost-sure termination.
why: It establishes that randomized software actually finishes with probability one, giving rigorous assurance for programs whose termination cannot be decided by testing or qualitative reasoning.
key_works: Chakarov and Sankaranarayanan (2014), *Expectation Invariants for Probabilistic Program Loops as Fixed Points*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-10936-7_6; *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem* (2019), arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Tight certified expected-runtime bounds
open: Can we automatically infer upper *and* lower bounds on the expected runtime of probabilistic loops — beyond merely deciding whether they terminate — in the presence of state-dependent distributions and nested recursion?
status: Expectation-based program analyses exist, but tightness, automation, and applicability to realistic recursive programs remain separate, unrealized targets. Key works include Chakarov and Sankaranarayanan (2014), DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-10936-7_6, and *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem*, arXiv:1910.12634; related algorithm-analysis work targets tight bounds for randomized recursion.
solved_when: An analysis exists that infers both useful upper and lower expected-runtime bounds, handles state-dependent distributions and nested recursion, and works automatically on realistic recursive probabilistic programs.
why: Such bounds tie probabilistic correctness to concrete cost and service-level planning, turning termination arguments into quantitative resource guarantees.
key_works: Chakarov and Sankaranarayanan (2014), DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-10936-7_6; *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem*, arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Sound automatic use of optional stopping
open: Can an automated verifier decide, soundly and without human intervention, when an optional-stopping argument applies to a probabilistic program? Concretely, this requires synthesizing and discharging side conditions such as integrability and boundedness, and rejecting proofs for which they fail.
status: The optional-stopping theorem itself is established; the open target is identifying and proving its applicability inside automated program verification. Key work: *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem* (2019), arXiv:1910.12634. Related: probability — effective uniform-integrability criteria.
solved_when: A tool exists that, given a probabilistic program and a proposed optional-stopping proof, automatically verifies the required side conditions (including integrability and boundedness) and rejects invalid proofs — with no manual proof of applicability.
why: It closes the gap between elegant martingale-style arguments and actually sound ones, preventing invalid probabilistic proofs from passing verification.
key_works: *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem* (2019), arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Proof certificates for learned probabilistic invariants
open: Can a learned invariant for a probabilistic program be paired with an independently checkable proof certificate that certifies it over all relevant states, not just the executions the learner sampled? In other words, can data-driven invariant discovery be combined with symbolic validation whose guarantee is universal rather than statistical?
status: Data-driven invariant learning for probabilistic programs has demonstrated progress, notably in Bao et al. (2025), *Data-Driven Invariant Learning for Probabilistic Programs* (DOI:10.1007/s10703-024-00466-x); what remains open is reliable certificate production that survives distribution and program changes.
solved_when: A pipeline exists that takes a learned probabilistic invariant and produces a certificate reliably verifiable by symbolic means, and this certificate production remains reliable under changes to the distribution and to the program itself.
why: It lets verification exploit statistical discovery of good invariant candidates without a sampling-based success being mistaken for — or silently turned into — a false universal guarantee of the program's behavior.
key_works: Bao et al. (2025), *Data-Driven Invariant Learning for Probabilistic Programs*, DOI:10.1007/s10703-024-00466-x.

title: Practical indefinite-horizon POMDP verification
open: Can we compute tight, certified bounds on the behavior of large partially observable Markov decision processes over indefinite horizons — with explicit error gaps whenever the exact solution is out of reach?
status: Verification methods for indefinite-horizon POMDPs exist, notably Bork, Junges, Katoen, and Quatmann (2020), *Verification of Indefinite-Horizon POMDPs*, and tool support in the Storm model checker; scaling belief-state reasoning and tightening the resulting bounds remain active targets.
solved_when: A verification method exists that scales belief-state reasoning to large POMDPs and returns certified bounds, together with explicit gaps, for indefinite-horizon properties, with tightness matching the best known bounds.
why: It underpins correct-by-construction agents and controllers that must act without observing the full state, from robotic planning to reactive control.
key_works: Bork, Junges, Katoen, and Quatmann (2020), *Verification of Indefinite-Horizon POMDPs*; Storm publications.

title: Probabilistic certificates robust to model uncertainty
open: When a system's transition probabilities are learned from data rather than known exactly, how can we verify guarantees over an explicitly defined uncertainty set for those probabilities? The question is to develop verification methods that soundly account for the estimation of the uncertainty set itself from finite data.
status: Probabilistic model checking (e.g., Dehnert et al. (2017), *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311) assumes a model is given; statistical estimation and formal verification (cf. Seshia et al. (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514) currently must be connected rather than conflated. Related statistical machinery exists in the form of distributionally robust confidence regions.
solved_when: A verification method exists that establishes probabilistic guarantees over explicitly defined uncertainty sets of transition probabilities, with the uncertainty-set estimation from finite data accounted for in the soundness of the certificate.
why: It makes numerical verification guarantees meaningful when probabilities are learned from observations rather than assumed known.
key_works: Dehnert et al. (2017), *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311; Seshia et al. (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Certified rare-event probabilities at practical cost
open: Can we estimate or bound extremely small failure probabilities using variance reduction, while still providing independently checkable justification that bias is controlled and confidence intervals have valid coverage?
status: Numerical model checking and statistical methods provide the foundations, but very rare events make naive simulation inadequate and make model assumptions especially consequential. Key works include *The Probabilistic Model Checker Storm* (2021), DOI:10.1007/s10009-021-00633-z, and PRISM project documentation.
solved_when: A method exists that produces rare-event probability estimates or bounds with variance reduction, together with certificates or arguments that can be independently checked for bias control and confidence coverage, at a cost practical enough to apply to realistic systems.
why: It would let reliability claims stand on evidence for failures so unlikely they would never appear during ordinary testing, instead of on unchecked assumptions.
key_works: *The Probabilistic Model Checker Storm* (2021), DOI:10.1007/s10009-021-00633-z; PRISM project documentation.

title: Compositional multiobjective probability bounds
open: Can we verify a system built from verified components and still obtain meaningful joint guarantees on failure probability, expected cost, and deadline satisfaction, when the components may be statistically dependent? Formally, the goal is a compositional framework that yields sound multiobjective bounds without assuming independence between components.
status: Multiobjective verification methods for MDPs and Markov automata exist, notably Markov automata with multiple objectives (Quatmann, Junges, and Katoen, 2017) and multi-cost bounded reachability in MDPs (Hartmanns et al., 2018), but scalable composition that avoids unjustified independence assumptions remains a distinct challenge.
solved_when: A compositional method exists that combines verified component specifications into joint bounds on failure probability, expected cost, and deadline satisfaction, and remains sound under arbitrary dependence between components.
why: Individually acceptable components can combine into a system that violates its overall guarantees; a sound compositional method prevents this without over-conservative or unjustified independence assumptions.
key_works: Quatmann, Junges, and Katoen (2017), *Markov Automata with Multiple Objectives*; Hartmanns et al. (2018), *Multi-Cost Bounded Reachability in MDP*.

title: Detecting vacuous industrial specifications
open: Can we automatically determine when a formally proved property is, in fact, vacuous — satisfied only because the underlying assumptions are inconsistent, the preconditions exclude the intended use cases, or the postcondition omits the very behavior it was meant to specify? The goal is a tool that flags such "proved the wrong thing" cases in industrial-scale deductive verification projects without human inspection of each proof.
status: Mutation analysis and specification testing provide partial evidence of specification adequacy; proof success itself does not establish adequacy. Key works include Celik et al. (2019), *Mutation Analysis for Coq*, and Jain et al. (2020), *mCoq: Mutation Analysis for Coq Verification Projects*.
solved_when: An automatic method exists that identifies proved properties whose satisfaction is trivial or irrelevant due to inconsistent assumptions, over-restrictive preconditions, or uninformative postconditions, and that demonstrably works on industrial verification projects.
why: A proof of the wrong property gives false assurance: the verifier believes the system is verified when the guarantee is empty. Detecting vacuity closes the gap between proof success and actual specification adequacy.
key_works: Celik et al. (2019), *Mutation Analysis for Coq*; Jain et al. (2020), *mCoq: Mutation Analysis for Coq Verification Projects*.

title: Requirement-to-formal-specification fidelity
open: Can we build a practical workflow that starts from an informal requirements document and ends with a formal specification demonstrably faithful to what stakeholders actually meant — exposing ambiguities along the way and recording how each was resolved?
status: This is a proposed scoped target, not a universal solution to informal meaning; existing formal verification establishes conformance to formal specifications, not automatic correctness of the specification choice. Related work spans faithful semantic parsing in NLP and ambiguity resolution in requirements engineering. Key references: Clarke and Wing et al. (1996), *Formal Methods: State of the Art and Future Directions*, DOI:10.1145/242223.242257; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652.
solved_when: A workflow exists that (i) surfaces ambiguities in the informal requirements, (ii) records explicit stakeholder resolutions of those ambiguities, and (iii) includes a test or procedure for checking that the resulting formal specification faithfully represents an independently written requirement.
why: Formal verification today certifies conformance to a formal specification, not that the specification itself captures user intent; this bridges that gap and connects mathematical assurance to actual user intent.
key_works: Clarke and Wing et al. (1996), *Formal Methods: State of the Art and Future Directions*, DOI:10.1145/242223.242257; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Usable semantic coverage metrics
open: How can we measure which meaningful behaviors a formal specification actually constrains, in a way that is usable in practice and does not reduce to counting proofs or annotation volume? The goal is to define and empirically validate semantic coverage metrics that capture the behavioral obligations a specification imposes.
status: Mutation-based approaches provide a baseline, but a broadly validated semantic coverage measure remains a research target.
solved_when: A semantic coverage metric is defined that (i) measures which meaningful behaviors a specification constrains without relying on proof count or annotation volume, and (ii) is validated broadly enough to serve as a general-purpose adequacy measure rather than a single-case experiment.
why: It would let practitioners distinguish substantial verification from superficial assurance, the way test adequacy criteria do in software testing.
key_works: Celik et al. (2019), *Mutation Analysis for Coq*; Jain et al. (2020), *mCoq*.

bib.title: Usable semantic coverage metrics

title: Automatic contracts for stateful external APIs
open: Can we automatically infer usable contracts for external APIs whose observable behavior depends on hidden state — rate limits, retry semantics, version changes — and then keep the inferred assumptions honest by validating and repairing them against actual observations?
status: Deductive tools support contracts, but undocumented external behavior of external services lies outside their proof boundary unless it is explicitly modeled; related work includes the Why3 project documentation and Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417, and system identification offers a relevant approach to learning reliable models of black-box services.
solved_when: A method exists that infers candidate contracts for stateful external APIs from observation and validates/maintains the explicit assumptions against runtime behavior, so undocumented external behavior is brought inside the deductive proof boundary without manual modeling.
why: It makes deductive verification applicable to service-oriented software that depends on third-party services whose internals cannot be inspected.
key_works: Why3 project documentation; Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417.

title: Exception-safe functional verification
open: Can a single, reusable specification discipline verify a production library's full behavior — normal results, exceptions, cancellation, cleanup, and partial initialization — rather than treating each as a separate proof effort? The goal is one consistent end-to-end discipline that works across realistic language and library boundaries.
status: Program logics and verified systems currently address subsets of this behavior; no existing approach gives consistent end-to-end treatment across realistic language and library boundaries. Key works include Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*, and Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422.
solved_when: A reusable specification discipline demonstrates consistent end-to-end verification of normal results, exceptions, cancellation, cleanup, and partial initialization for production libraries.
why: Many operational failures occur on exceptional paths rather than the main algorithm, so verification that ignores these paths misses precisely where systems break in practice.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422.

title: Modular proof of algorithmic complexity contracts
open: Can we prove asymptotic and concrete cost contracts for verified code in a way that survives composition — remaining valid when clients compose libraries, change data representations, or invoke callbacks?
status: Verified implementations and cost reasoning exist, notably in the CakeML project and publications and in work such as Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement*, arXiv:1701.05888; however, stable library-level complexity interfaces remain an open integration target.
solved_when: A deductive verification framework exists in which cost contracts (both asymptotic and concrete) are proved once at the library level and remain valid under client composition, data-representation changes, and callback invocation.
why: Without modularity, performance guarantees proved for a component are silently invalidated the moment a client composes it differently, so verified abstraction cannot be trusted to preserve cost behavior.
key_works: CakeML project and publications; Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement*, arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Minimal sufficient annotations without weaker specifications
open: Can the human-written annotation burden of a deductive verification workflow be reduced while the program semantics and the intended specification are held fixed — that is, without making the verification task easier by weakening preconditions or deleting proof obligations?
status: LLM-assisted Dafny systems already improve proof automation (Banerjee, Bouissou, and Zetzsche (2026), *DafnyPro: LLM-Assisted Automated Verification for Dafny Programs*, arXiv:2601.05385), but specification-preserving annotation reduction remains the open target; the risk of reward-hacking-style shortcut behavior is known from machine learning work on automated coding benchmarks.
solved_when: An automated tool demonstrably reduces required human annotations on a fixed program and specification, with checks in place that preconditions are not weakened and no verification obligations are removed.
why: It cuts the labor cost of deductive verification without gaming the task, so measured gains reflect real automation rather than a quietly easier proof problem.
key_works: Banerjee, Bouissou, and Zetzsche (2026), *DafnyPro: LLM-Assisted Automated Verification for Dafny Programs*, arXiv:2601.05385.

title: Specification-preserving automated program repair
open: Can an automated repair system fix a defective program while provably preserving its original specification — including required behavior — and confining changes to the defect rather than rippling elsewhere?
status: Specification-guided repair has been demonstrated only in restricted settings, e.g., Wu, Mendes, and Abreu (2025), *Specification-Guided Repair of Arithmetic Errors in Dafny Programs Using LLMs*, arXiv:2507.03659. Broad semantic preservation and reliable repair generalization remain open engineering targets.
solved_when: A repair tool exists that, given an incorrect program and its formal specification, produces a corrected program together with a proof that the specification still holds, required behavior is preserved, and modifications outside the defect site are bounded; generalization to unrestricted program settings (beyond restricted domains such as arithmetic errors in Dafny) is demonstrated.
why: It would turn formal specifications from static checklists into a safe mechanism for automated software maintenance, letting repairs be applied without fear of regressions or unintended semantic drift.
key_works: Wu, Mendes, and Abreu (2025), *Specification-Guided Repair of Arithmetic Errors in Dafny Programs Using LLMs*, arXiv:2507.03659.

title: Compositional starvation-freedom under realistic schedulers
open: Can starvation-freedom be proved compositionally under scheduler assumptions that a real runtime can actually honor? The goal is a liveness account whose fairness conditions — including priorities and bounded interference — are justified by deployed scheduling policies rather than stipulated abstractly.
status: Fairness-based termination logics exist, but connecting the logical fairness assumptions they rely on to deployed scheduling policies remains an unmet, distinct obligation.
solved_when: A compositional proof of starvation-freedom exists whose scheduler assumptions (priorities, bounded interference) can be shown to hold for an actual runtime's scheduling policy, rather than assumed.
why: Without this, liveness proofs assume away the operational failure mode — starvation under real schedulers — and give no guarantee for deployed systems.
key_works: D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*, DOI:10.1145/3477082; Tassarotti et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Cancellation-safe concurrent protocols
open: Can a concurrent protocol be designed and verified so that cancelling an operation at any permitted suspension point is safe — that is, cancellation preserves ownership invariants, releases the canceller's outstanding obligations, and cannot permanently block other participants?
status: Separation logics already support sophisticated ownership reasoning, but cancellation introduces nonlocal control effects and progress obligations that require additional treatment beyond current frameworks; key foundations include Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*, and D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.
solved_when: A protocol specification and proof (e.g., in a separation-logic framework) exist showing that cancellation at every permitted suspension point preserves ownership, discharges obligations, and rules out permanent blocking of other participants.
why: Cancellation is a common failure mode in asynchronous services: without such guarantees, a cancelled operation can leak resources, leave dangling obligations, or deadlock its peers.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: Weak-memory liveness without unjustified fairness transfer
open: Under what reusable conditions does a source-level progress proof still hold after compilation to weak-memory hardware? Formally, identify compositional criteria guaranteeing that liveness established under strongly-ordered semantics is preserved by compilation to relaxed-memory machines.
status: Weak-memory semantics and concurrent termination logics have advanced separately (Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850; Tassarotti et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.05888), but safety-preserving compilation alone does not establish liveness preservation.
solved_when: A set of reusable conditions is established under which source-level termination or progress proofs provably survive compilation to weak-memory hardware — covering both the compilation scheme and the fairness/forward-progress assumptions on the target.
why: Without it, a terminating source proof can mask a hardware-level execution that spins or starves, so verified concurrent programs offer no real progress guarantee on actual machines.
key_works: Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850; Tassarotti et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.05888.

bib.title: Weak-memory liveness without unjustified fairness transfer

title: Verified scalable memory reclamation
open: Can we build a machine-checked verification of a practical memory reclamation scheme that holds up under the full conditions of real concurrent systems — weak memory consistency, thread failure, cancellation, and dynamically registered readers — proving both safety and reclamation progress?
status: Foundational ownership and weak-memory frameworks exist — notably Iris (Jung et al., 2018, *Iris from the Ground Up*) and promising semantics for relaxed-memory concurrency (Kang et al., 2017) — but their combined operational envelope for this problem remains the target.
solved_when: A practical reclamation scheme is formally verified under weak memory, thread failure, cancellation, and dynamically registered readers, with proofs of both safety and reclamation progress.
why: It would enable safe high-performance concurrent containers without unbounded growth of retired memory.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*.

title: Compositional linearizability across foreign-function boundaries
open: Can we prove linearizability of a concurrent library whose implementation spans multiple languages, memory models, and calling conventions — and do so compositionally, with explicit ownership and callback contracts at each foreign-function boundary?
status: Language-local logics and source-level concurrency models do not automatically compose across foreign-function interfaces; no compositional account spanning such boundaries currently exists. Key works: Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*.
solved_when: A formal framework exists that establishes linearizability for concurrent components crossing foreign-function interfaces, treating ownership transfer and callback contracts explicitly, and composing proofs across the differing source-level concurrency models of the participating languages.
why: Real high-performance libraries are assembled precisely this way — from components written in different languages — so verification that stops at each foreign-function boundary cannot certify the systems practitioners actually ship.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*.

title: Crash-and-concurrency liveness
open: Prove that a concurrent service eventually resumes useful work after repeated but suitably bounded crashes, including cleanup of abandoned locks and obligations.
status: Perennial addresses concurrent crash safety, while IronFleet and TaDA Live address important liveness settings; their combined recovery-progress target requires more than safety composition.
solved_when: A proof exists that, under suitably bounded crash patterns, the service is guaranteed to eventually resume useful work — covering recovery and cleanup of abandoned locks and outstanding obligations.
why: A service that safely remains stuck is not operationally correct; liveness under crashes is what makes recovery actually useful.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Verifying Concurrent, Crash-Safe Systems with Perennial*, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: Automated refinement between concurrent implementations
open: Can we automatically prove that an optimized concurrent implementation refines a simpler reference implementation, tracking not only functional behavior but also observable progress and resource behavior?
status: Higher-order termination-preserving refinement has a logical foundation, following Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement* (arXiv:1701.05888), but large-scale automatic discovery of simulation relations remains an open target.
solved_when: A tool automatically establishes refinement between concurrent implementations and their reference specifications, preserving termination and resource behavior, with automatic discovery of the needed simulation relations at large scale.
why: It would permit aggressive optimization of concurrent code while keeping an understandable specification that users can trust.
key_works: Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement*, arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Complete mechanized Rust semantic integration
open: Can the many facets of Rust's behavior — ownership, unsafe code, aliasing, concurrency, panics, and the rest of the language — be brought together in a single maintained mechanized semantics that program proofs and compiler validation can build on?
status: RustBelt (Jung et al., 2018), MiniRust (Jung, 2025, *The Current State of MiniRust*), Tree Borrows, and RefinedRust (Gäher et al., 2024) each address substantial pieces of the problem; the remaining task is integration, not building formal foundations for Rust from scratch.
solved_when: A maintained, mechanized semantics of Rust integrates ownership, unsafe code, aliasing, concurrency, panics, and the relevant language features, and demonstrably supports program proofs and compiler validation.
why: It would give different Rust verification tools a coherent semantic reference to share, instead of each resting on its own fragmentary foundations.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*; Jung (2025), *The Current State of MiniRust*; Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*.

title: Unsafe Rust proofs respecting executable aliasing restrictions
open: Can we verify substantial unsafe Rust libraries against a precise aliasing model, so that alias validity is established inside the proof rather than left outside the argument while only functional properties are verified?
status: Tree Borrows (Villani et al., 2025, DOI:10.1145/3735592) supplies a developed aliasing model, and 2026 work by Tas and Jacobs (arXiv:2603.28326) explicitly advances modular verification of unsafe Rust against Rust's pointer-aliasing restrictions; verifying full substantial libraries against such a model remains open.
solved_when: A verification of a substantial unsafe Rust library exists in which conformance to a precise pointer-aliasing model (e.g., Tree Borrows) is proved, not assumed, alongside the library's functional properties.
why: Without it, proofs certify executions that the Rust language nevertheless considers undefined — the verification is sound about behavior but silent about whether the aliased pointer use is legal at all.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*, DOI:10.1145/3735592; Tas and Jacobs (2026), *Towards Verifying Unsafe Rust Programs against Rust’s Pointer-Aliasing Restrictions*, arXiv:2603.28326.

title: Sound alias-model evolution without ecosystem breakage
open: How can a programming language change its aliasing model — for example, tighten the rules under which pointer reuse is permitted — while compiler soundness is proven and the set of previously accepted programs that become invalid is identified systematically?
status: Tree Borrows includes substantial empirical and formal evaluation, but general migration guarantees across model revisions remain a separate target. Key works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*, DOI:10.1145/3735592; Jung (2023), *From Stacks to Trees*.
solved_when: A general method exists for evolving an aliasing model that both carries a compiler soundness proof and systematically determines which existing programs are invalidated by the change; migration guarantees across model revisions are established.
why: It makes semantic improvements compatible with a large existing ecosystem, so languages can fix unsound or awkward aliasing semantics without silently breaking working programs.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*, DOI:10.1145/3735592; Jung (2023), *From Stacks to Trees*.
