title: Out-of-thin-air-free semantics with useful global optimizations
open: Can we give a semantics for relaxed-memory concurrency that both forbids out-of-thin-air reads and still permits the aggressive global optimizations real compilers perform? Formally, the challenge is a single operational or axiomatic model that simultaneously rules out fabricated values, validates useful global optimizations, and supports compositional reasoning about realistic programs.
status: Promising semantics (Kang et al., 2017, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850) and Promising 2.0 (Lee et al., 2020, *Promising 2.0: Global Optimizations in Relaxed Memory Concurrency*) are major partial solutions. The remaining target is coverage, implementation alignment, and reusable verification interfaces, not the absence of candidate semantics.
solved_when: A semantics is given that demonstrably avoids out-of-thin-air behavior, soundly supports aggressive (global) compiler optimizations, and yields compositional reasoning principles for realistic relaxed-memory programs — with acceptable coverage of realistic language features and alignment with actual implementations.
why: Without it, we must choose between trustworthy concurrent reasoning (no fabricated values) and performant compilers; a solution gives both sound optimization and reliable verification of concurrent code.
key_works: Kang et al. (2017), DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850; Lee et al. (2020), *Promising 2.0: Global Optimizations in Relaxed Memory Concurrency*.

bib.title: Out-of-thin-air-free semantics with useful global optimizations

title: Verified async lowering with pinning and cancellation
open: Does the standard lowering of asynchronous programs into state machines — the transformation at the heart of async/await compilation — provably preserve ownership, pinning, cancellation behavior, and observable program results?
status: Rust verification foundations and compiler-level models provide components; a complete treatment of this combined transformation is the proposed target. Relevant groundwork includes Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422, and Jung (2025), *The Current State of MiniRust*.
solved_when: A machine-checked or rigorous formal proof exists showing that the lowering of asynchronous programs into state machines preserves ownership, pinning, cancellation behavior, and observable results.
why: Async/await is a dominant style of systems programming; a verified lowering gives concrete correctness guarantees for compiled async code, from memory safety to cancellation semantics.
key_works: Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422; Jung (2025), *The Current State of MiniRust*.

bib.title: Verified async lowering with pinning and cancellation

title: Empirical conformance testing for formal language semantics
open: Can we build and maintain a living corpus that empirically checks whether formal semantics, interpreters, compiler outputs, and real hardware actually agree on what programs should do, with disagreements minimized and expected behavior adjudicated by the community?
status: Tree Borrows (Villani et al., 2025) and Cerberus (Memarian, 2023, *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981) have demonstrated the value of empirical validation of formal semantics; the target is an ongoing multi-tool semantic observatory extending this approach.
solved_when: A continuously maintained "semantic observatory" exists that compares formal semantics against interpreters, compiler outputs, and hardware, with reported disagreements minimized and expected-behavior outcomes explicitly adjudicated.
why: Such a corpus detects drift between mathematical models of language semantics and the implementations actually deployed, before that drift becomes unsoundness in real compilers or hardware.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*; Memarian (2023), *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981.

bib.title: Empirical conformance testing for formal language semantics

title: Unbounded translation validation for optimizing compiler pipelines
open: Can we build a translation validator that certifies loop and recursion transformations — such as optimizations restructuring unbounded loops or recursive functions — without relying on fixed unrolling bounds, and that emits a simulation argument an independent checker can verify?
status: Alive2 (Lopes et al. 2021, *Alive2: Bounded Translation Validation for LLVM*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030) provides powerful bounded translation validation for LLVM, but extending coverage to unbounded transformations remains a different, open problem. Related work includes automated discovery of relational invariants for program equivalence.
solved_when: A validator exists that handles unbounded loop and recursion transformations and produces independently checkable simulation proofs, rather than depending solely on bounded unrolling.
why: It would find or rule out optimization bugs that only manifest beyond bounded executions, where current bounded validators are blind.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2: Bounded Translation Validation for LLVM*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030.

bib.title: Unbounded translation validation for optimizing compiler pipelines

title: Verified optimizing compilation for broader production-language coverage
open: Can a fully verified optimizing compiler cover a realistic modern language toolchain — concurrency model, runtime system, exception semantics, and foreign-function interface included — rather than a curated core language? Formally: extend the verified-compilation envelope to a declared production-language surface with all of these features mechanized end to end.
status: CompCert and CakeML already demonstrate verified compilers, so the goal is broader feature coverage with competitive optimization, not "the first verified compiler." Key works: Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*; CompCert 3.18 documentation (2026); CakeML project.
solved_when: A verified compiler exists whose soundness theorem covers the full declared envelope of the target language/toolchain, including its concurrency, runtime, exception, and foreign-function features, while performing optimizations competitive with unverified production compilers.
why: It closes the gap between the source language whose behavior is verified and the executable actually run in production, so verified guarantees stop eroding at the boundary of unsupported features.
key_works: Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*; CompCert 3.18 documentation (2026); CakeML project.

bib.title: Verified optimizing compilation for broader production-language coverage

title: Verified dynamic linking and plugin loading
open: Can a system load, replace, or unload code at runtime while provably preserving the guarantees of every component involved, including symbol resolution, callbacks, and ownership of shared state?
status: Verified compiler and systems projects, including the CompCert project and publications and the work surveyed in Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627, establish substantial static foundations; however, dynamic composition adds obligations not implied by a compiler-correctness theorem.
solved_when: A verified mechanism for dynamic linking and plugin loading exists whose correctness proof covers symbol resolution, callback safety, and shared-state ownership across load, replacement, and unload operations at runtime.
why: Plugin-based and hot-updated production systems already rely on exactly this kind of dynamic composition, so a verified foundation would give them the same assurance that verified compilers give to statically linked code.
key_works: CompCert project and publications; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

bib.title: Verified dynamic linking and plugin loading

title: Verified JIT deoptimization
open: Can a just-in-time compiler's deoptimization path be proved safe — showing that speculative optimization, guard failure, stack reconstruction, and deoptimization jointly preserve the program's observable behavior under realistic runtime state?
status: Static compiler correctness (Leroy 2009, *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*) and bounded translation validation (Lopes et al. 2021, *Alive2*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030) supply useful techniques, but the entire adaptive runtime transition remains unverified and is the target.
solved_when: A mechanically verified proof exists that the full adaptive transition — from speculative optimized code through guard failure to reconstructed interpreter/compiled state — preserves observable behavior for all runtime states reachable in a realistic execution engine.
why: Deoptimization is the safety net that makes speculative optimization viable; without a verified guarantee, adaptive execution engines carry correctness risks that no static compiler proof covers.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030; Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*.

title: Verified GPU compilation across memory hierarchies
open: Can we build a verified compilation pipeline for GPU kernels that preserves source-level semantics all the way to the device, in the presence of the full heterogeneous memory hierarchy — shared memory, barriers, atomics, subgroup operations, and host/device transfers?
status: Compiler and ISA semantics address important ingredients; the proposed target combines concurrency semantics with heterogeneous execution. Key works include Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS*, DOI:10.1145/3290384, and Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*.
solved_when: A verification of source-to-device semantic preservation exists for kernels exercising shared memory, barriers, atomics, subgroup operations, and host/device transfers.
why: It extends formal assurance to the accelerators that dominate scientific and AI workloads, where unverified compilation currently leaves a gap between verified host code and executed device code.
key_works: Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS*, DOI:10.1145/3290384; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*.

title: Semantic preservation of profile-guided optimization
open: Can we certify that profile-guided optimization preserves program semantics even when the profile data is stale or adversarial — that is, prove that a profile may steer performance decisions but can never license an unjustified semantic assumption?
status: Translation validation supplies a promising baseline (Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030), but profile handling and speculative assumptions are not yet included in the checked boundary.
solved_when: A validation or certification mechanism exists whose checked boundary explicitly covers profile handling and speculative assumptions, and which proves semantic preservation for profile-guided optimizations under arbitrary (including adversarial) profiles.
why: It allows data-driven optimization without data-driven correctness, so compilers can exploit profile information aggressively without that information becoming a trusted input to semantics.

bib.title: Semantic preservation of profile-guided optimization

title: Verified garbage collection with concurrent foreign references
open: Can a moving or concurrent garbage collector be proven correct when the managed heap is entangled with a foreign world — external pointers held by unverified code, callbacks crossing the boundary, safepoints, and weak-memory synchronization all in play at once?
status: Verified language runtimes have demonstrated important collector foundations, but cross-language concurrent roots substantially enlarge the proof boundary. Key works include the CakeML project's verified runtime and compiler publications and Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.
solved_when: A mechanically verified correctness proof exists for a moving or concurrent collector that soundly handles foreign pointers, callbacks, safepoints, and weak-memory synchronization simultaneously.
why: It removes a major runtime assumption currently made by high-level program proofs, letting verified programs rely on collectors that interact with unverified foreign code without unproven gaps.
key_works: CakeML project, verified runtime and compiler publications; Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.

bib.title: Verified garbage collection with concurrent foreign references

title: Proof-preserving reproducible builds
open: Can we build a full toolchain in which a proof carried out against the source is preserved all the way to a reproducible executable artifact, accounting for build scripts, generated code, linker behavior, tool versions, and dependency selection? Formally, the goal is a construction that ties verified compilation to reproducible-build provenance as a single end-to-end obligation.
status: Verified compilation, as in Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*, the CakeML project, and Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627, proves a semantic relation for a particular pipeline; reproducible-build provenance remains an additional end-to-end obligation not subsumed by it.
solved_when: A working pipeline exists that connects source proofs to reproducible executables while accounting for build scripts, generated code, linker behavior, tool versions, and dependency selection — verified compilation alone is insufficient, since reproducible-build provenance must be discharged as an additional end-to-end obligation.
why: It guarantees that the deployed binary is the binary covered by the proof — closing the gap between what was verified and what actually ships.
key_works: Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*; CakeML project; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627.

bib.title: Proof-preserving reproducible builds

title: End-to-end assurance across kernel hardware assumptions
open: Can a substantially larger fraction of a verified kernel's assumptions about the underlying platform — boot code, devices, DMA, and general hardware behavior — be discharged by proof or brought under explicit, machine-checked monitoring at run time? In other words, can the boundary between what is verified and what is merely assumed be pushed outward toward the physical hardware?
status: seL4 has extensive proofs, and its AArch64 security proofs were completed in August 2026 (seL4 Foundation, 2026, *Verification* documentation and linked assumptions; Klein et al. 2018, DOI:10.1145/3230627). The remaining target concerns the surrounding assumptions, not that already completed milestone.
solved_when: A significantly larger share of kernel assumptions concerning boot code, devices, DMA, and hardware behavior are either formally discharged or explicitly monitored, with each remaining assumption documented and tracked rather than silently trusted.
why: Kernel verification is only as strong as its trust base; without this, assurance stops at the kernel's interface to hardware. Discharging or monitoring these assumptions extends the guarantee to the actually deployed platform.
key_works: seL4 Foundation (2026), *Verification* documentation and linked assumptions; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627.

bib.title: End-to-end assurance across kernel hardware assumptions

title: Verified high-performance device drivers
open: Can a production-grade device driver be formally verified against a device model that faithfully captures the messy parts of real hardware — interrupts, DMA, reset, timeouts, and documented error behavior — while retaining high performance? Formally: a correctness proof relating the driver implementation to a device specification covering all of these behaviors, not just the happy path.
status: Verified-system deployments, including seL4-based work surveyed by Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627, establish the feasibility of verified software in production, but driver/device interfaces remain a major source of assumptions and integration work; complete executable device specifications remain an open hardware-engineering problem.
solved_when: A driver used in production is verified against a device model that includes interrupts, DMA, reset, timeout, and documented error behavior, with no unverifiable assumptions at the driver/device interface.
why: Drivers are the privileged components most often left outside the verified perimeter; verifying them against realistic device models closes that gap and shrinks the trusted computing base of verified systems.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627; seL4 verification assumptions.

bib.title: Verified high-performance device drivers

title: Verified IOMMU and DMA isolation
open: Can device assignment to a guest or driver be proven safe end-to-end, so that a peripheral's DMA cannot breach memory isolation? Formally: prove isolation across the full path of device assignment, IOMMU configuration, address translation, stale mappings, and device reset.
status: Existing kernel isolation proofs do not automatically cover unrestricted DMA behavior; the target must include both configuration software and a defensible device model. Key works: seL4 Foundation, *Verification* and assumptions documentation; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.
solved_when: A verified proof of isolation exists covering device assignment, IOMMU configuration, address translation, stale mappings, and device reset, and it encompasses both the configuration software and a defensible device model.
why: Without it, peripheral access can silently invalidate the memory-isolation guarantees that kernel isolation proofs establish, so a malicious or misconfigured device defeats the whole verification story.
key_works: seL4 Foundation, *Verification* and assumptions documentation; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

bib.title: Verified IOMMU and DMA isolation

title: Verified live migration with isolation and continuity
open: Does there exist a machine-checked proof that a virtual machine or sandbox can be migrated while running without violating state consistency, isolation guarantees, or externally visible execution semantics, even when failures occur mid-migration?
status: Existing work on verified kernels and distributed crash reasoning (e.g., Klein et al., 2018, DOI:10.1145/3230627; Chajed et al., 2019, Perennial, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632) provides the foundations; migration is the step that joins these domains with device and network state.
solved_when: A verified migration mechanism exists with a formal, machine-checked proof covering preservation of relevant state, isolation, and externally visible execution semantics across failures during live migration.
why: It would enable trustworthy maintenance and load balancing of verified services, so operational actions on a running system no longer void its verification guarantees.

bib.title: Verified live migration with isolation and continuity

title: Temporal isolation with shared microarchitectural resources
open: Can we prove useful timing-isolation bounds for software components that share microarchitectural resources such as caches, interconnects, memory controllers, and accelerators?
status: Existing functional and information-flow kernel proofs (e.g., the seL4 verification) do not by themselves establish precise shared-resource timing guarantees; tools like Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR* (arXiv:1812.08639), address related timing-channel concerns, and compositional worst-case interference analysis from real-time systems is a related line of work.
solved_when: A formal framework exists that establishes quantitative timing-isolation bounds for components sharing these microarchitectural resources, going beyond what functional and information-flow kernel proofs provide.
why: It would support real-time assurance and timing-channel control in systems where functional correctness alone does not constrain interference.
key_works: seL4 verification documentation; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*, arXiv:1812.08639.

bib.title: Temporal isolation with shared microarchitectural resources

title: Verified suspend/resume through real platform power transitions
open: Can we prove that an operating system preserves its state and its security guarantees across a full real-world power cycle — suspend, hibernation, resume, device reinitialization, and restoration that may be interrupted midway?
status: Existing kernel verification and crash-safe-system proofs, such as Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627, and Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*, supply pieces of the needed machinery, but no proof covers full platform power transitions, which cut across firmware, device, storage, and kernel boundaries at once.
solved_when: A verified system carries a machine-checked proof that state and security invariants are preserved across suspend, hibernation, resume, device reinitialization, and interrupted restoration, spanning the firmware, device, storage, and kernel boundaries those transitions cross.
why: It extends formal assurance from steady-state execution to the ordinary lifecycle operations every deployed system actually undergoes, closing a gap where today's guarantees silently stop.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*.

bib.title: Verified suspend/resume through real platform power transitions

title: Formally verified operational configuration
open: Can an operational system's runtime configuration — capabilities, mounts, namespaces, network policy, and startup settings — be mechanically checked against the isolation architecture its formal proofs assume? In other words, is there a verified configuration-to-theorem connection so that a deployed configuration provably instantiates the architecture under which the system's guarantees hold?
status: Verified components can currently be deployed under incorrect configurations; no checked configuration-to-theorem connection exists yet, though it is the stated target. Background comes from Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627, and seL4 deployment and verification documentation.
solved_when: A checked connection exists between concrete deployed configurations (covering capabilities, mounts, namespaces, network policy, and startup configuration) and the isolation architecture assumed by the system proofs, such that verified components can no longer be deployed under configurations that violate those assumptions.
why: Today a formally verified component can still be deployed under an incorrect configuration that silently bypasses its formal guarantees; a verified configuration link closes this gap between proof and operation.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627; seL4 deployment and verification documentation.

bib.title: Formally verified operational configuration

title: Low-cost verified platform maintenance
open: Can the engineering effort of maintaining a verified kernel-plus-runtime platform across hardware and compiler upgrades be reduced by at least 10× relative to a documented longitudinal baseline?
status: Proposed moonshot; existing deployments (e.g., Klein et al. 2018, DOI:10.1145/3230627; Huang et al. 2026, *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652) demonstrate feasibility but do not establish low ongoing migration cost.
solved_when: A verified platform is maintained across hardware and compiler upgrades with at least a 10× reduction in engineering effort, measured against a documented longitudinal baseline.
why: It makes verified platforms sustainable beyond a single funded release, so high-assurance infrastructure can be kept current without repeated major reinvestment.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

bib.title: Low-cost verified platform maintenance

title: Implementation-level consensus proofs with full operational envelopes
open: Can a real, production consensus implementation be fully verified — including serialization, storage, reconfiguration, recovery, and runtime behavior — under explicit network assumptions?
status: IronFleet (Hawblitzel et al., 2017, DOI:10.1145/3068608) and Grove (Sharma et al., 2023, arXiv:2309.03046) already verify substantial distributed implementations; the remaining target is broader operational coverage, not basic consensus verification.
solved_when: A verification of a production-grade consensus implementation covers all of serialization, storage, reconfiguration, recovery, and runtime behavior, with the network assumptions made explicit.
why: It closes the gap between an abstract consensus proof and an actually deployed service.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*, DOI:10.1145/3068608; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, arXiv:2309.03046.

bib.title: Implementation-level consensus proofs with full operational envelopes

title: Rolling-upgrade correctness with mixed protocol versions
open: Can a rolling upgrade be proven safe and eventually progressing while old and new protocol versions coexist in the same deployment? The question is to establish these guarantees in full generality, covering schema changes, rollback, and interrupted deployment.
status: Verified distributed systems supply the necessary components, but mixed-version operational transitions still require explicit compatibility relations to be specified; no such general proof currently exists. Related foundations include Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, DOI:10.1145/3600006.3613172, and Newcombe et al. (2015), DOI:10.1145/2699417.
solved_when: A proof (or machine-checked verification) exists of both safety and eventual progress for a system in which old- and new-version nodes coexist, explicitly handling schema changes, rollback paths, and interrupted (partially completed) deployments.
why: Routine deployment is when production systems are most exposed; a solution means the guarantees of a verified system survive the ordinary act of upgrading it, rather than holding only between releases.

bib.title: Rolling-upgrade correctness with mixed protocol versions

title: Verified leases with real clock behavior
open: Can we make the safety and liveness proofs of lease-based systems robust to how clocks actually behave on real platforms — drift, pauses, reboots, and bounded time-synchronization error? Concretely, this asks for lease correctness arguments tied formally to explicit assumptions about clock drift rates, pause durations, reboot behavior, and sync uncertainty.
status: Grove (Sharma et al., 2023, arXiv:2309.03046) already verifies lease-using systems; the proposed extension is a stronger connection to platform clock behavior and operational fault assumptions. Related parametric techniques appear in André (2019, arXiv:1907.00555).
solved_when: A verification of a lease-using system (e.g., in Grove) establishes safety and liveness under explicit, parameterized bounds on clock drift, pauses, reboot behavior, and time-synchronization uncertainty.
why: Without it, timing assumptions can silently undermine the ownership guarantees leases are meant to provide; with it, verified lease systems rest on operational fault assumptions a deployer can actually check.
key_works: Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, arXiv:2309.03046; André (2019), *Parametric Verification*, arXiv:1907.00555.

bib.title: Verified leases with real clock behavior

title: Compositional reconfiguration across multiple services
open: When several control planes — membership, sharding, authorization, and routing — reconfigure independently and their transitions overlap in time, does the composed system still preserve its global invariants throughout? A proof is needed that safety holds during overlapping reconfiguration, not only at stable points between changes.
status: Grove (Sharma et al., 2023, DOI:10.1145/3600006.3613172) demonstrates verified reconfiguration within substantial systems; composition of several independently changing control planes remains a broader, unaddressed target. Newcombe et al. (2015), *How AWS Uses Formal Methods*, documents industrial use of formal methods in this setting.
solved_when: A verified demonstration that independently reconfiguring membership, sharding, authorization, and routing preserves global invariants during overlapping transitions.
why: Modern infrastructure runs multiple concurrent controllers, so correctness must hold while they change at the same time — not only when each changes in isolation.
key_works: Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, DOI:10.1145/3600006.3613172; Newcombe et al. (2015), *How AWS Uses Formal Methods*.

bib.title: Compositional reconfiguration across multiple services

title: Verified retries across external side-effect boundaries
open: Can we give machine-checked guarantees that a workflow involving retries and crashes produces at-most-once or explicitly compensated external effects? The proof should state exactly which external systems are assumed to support idempotency or atomic commit, rather than assuming unconditional "exactly once" delivery.
status: Crash-safe and distributed proofs supply the foundations (e.g., Chajed et al. 2019, *Perennial*; Sharma et al. 2023, *Grove*); unconditional "exactly once" across arbitrary external services is explicitly not the target.
solved_when: A verified implementation of a retry-and-crash-prone workflow exists in which every external effect is proven to occur at most once or to be explicitly compensated, with the idempotency or atomic-commit assumptions about each external system made explicit.
why: Duplicated payments, messages, or provisioning actions are a real failure mode; this eliminates them by construction rather than by operational vigilance.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

bib.title: Verified retries across external side-effect boundaries

title: Mechanized consistency contracts for client libraries
open: Does a full client stack — retries, caches, sessions, and routing — preserve the consistency contract that a distributed storage service exports? Formally, extend the consistency theorem of a verified service across the client middleware layer so that the end-to-end guarantee holds.
status: The existing components come from server-side proofs and weak-isolation logics, but client middleware can introduce behaviors that fall outside a server-only theorem, so the end-to-end result remains unproven. Key works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115.
solved_when: A mechanized proof exists showing that client-side retries, caches, sessions, and routing, composed with the service, still satisfy the service's exported consistency contract end to end.
why: It makes the guarantee that applications actually observe match the guarantee the service claims to deliver, closing the gap between the exported contract and real client behavior.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115.

bib.title: Mechanized consistency contracts for client libraries

title: Progress proofs under backpressure and overload
open: Can we prove that realistic service-protocol machinery — bounded queues, admission control, retry policies, and resource pools — remains free of deadlock and pathological feedback loops when subjected to overload and backpressure under explicitly declared load assumptions?
status: Safety and liveness verification for distributed protocols exists (e.g., Hawblitzel et al., 2017, *IronFleet*; D’Osualdo et al., 2021, *TaDA Live*), but overload behavior and coupling between resources must be modeled explicitly rather than assumed away; queueing theory's study of stability in interacting retry and admission policies is a related line of work.
solved_when: A proof establishes deadlock-freedom (liveness) and absence of pathological feedback for protocols combining bounded queues, admission control, retry policies, and resource pools, under the declared load assumptions, with overload and resource coupling treated explicitly in the model.
why: It targets failures that surface only under operational stress, precisely the conditions production systems face but verification efforts typically assume away.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

bib.title: Progress proofs under backpressure and overload

title: Automatic refinement from design models to service code
open: Can we automatically maintain a verified refinement relation between a high-level protocol design model and its evolving service implementation, so that changes on either side — including serialization and failure-handling code — propagate without breaking the correspondence?
status: AWS reports substantial benefits from design-level formal methods (Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417), while implementation-verification systems such as Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*, establish another route; automatically connecting both remains a valuable target.
solved_when: A system exists that establishes and continuously maintains a checked mapping from design models to implementation code, covering serialization and failure handling, and keeping the relation valid as the code and models change over time.
why: Without such a connection, verified design models and shipped code drift apart, so the formal guarantees established at design time say nothing about the running service.
key_works: Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417; Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*.

bib.title: Automatic refinement from design models to service code

title: Crash proofs under realistic storage-device behavior
open: Can we verify recovery of a concurrent, crash-safe system against a storage model that reflects how real devices actually behave — including torn writes, write reordering, volatile device caches, flush semantics, and documented device failure behavior? The goal is to extend such a model and validate it against actual device contracts.
status: Perennial (Chajed et al., 2019, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632) establishes concurrent crash-safe verification. The remaining target is extending and validating its storage model against actual device contracts.
solved_when: A crash-safety verification framework exists whose storage model captures torn writes, reordering, volatile device caches, flush semantics, and documented device failure behavior, and the model has been validated against actual device contracts.
why: It prevents proofs from relying on storage guarantees the hardware does not provide, which would make verified systems unsafe in practice.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Verifying Concurrent, Crash-Safe Systems with Perennial*, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632.

bib.title: Crash proofs under realistic storage-device behavior

title: Verified online compaction and garbage collection
open: Can we build a concurrent storage compaction and garbage collection procedure with a machine-checked proof that it preserves the logical contents of storage and remains recoverable across interruption, crash, and restart — while still making progress reclaiming space?
status: Crash-safe concurrent program logics — e.g., Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*, and D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live* — provide the foundations, but achieving the combined safety, recovery, and reclamation-progress target remains workload-specific engineering.
solved_when: A verified implementation exists whose proof establishes logical-content preservation, crash and restart recovery, and eventual space reclamation under concurrent access.
why: Without it, background maintenance can silently corrupt data or, failing that, exhaust storage under sustained writes.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: End-to-end SQL optimizer equivalence
open: Can we build an equivalence checker that certifies query rewrites end-to-end across a declared production fragment of SQL, including duplicates, NULL semantics, aggregates, ordering where it is semantically relevant, and supported user-defined functions?
status: Cosette and U-semiring-based work, notably Chu et al. (2018), *Axiomatic Foundations and Algorithms for Deciding Semantic Equivalences of SQL Queries* (DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200), establish substantial equivalence-checking results; complete production-language coverage remains a broader target.
solved_when: A checker exists that decides semantic equivalence for the full declared fragment — covering duplicates, NULL behavior, aggregates, ordering where relevant, and supported UDFs — and certifies optimizer rewrites within it.
why: It prevents silent wrong-result query optimizations, where an optimizer transformation quietly returns incorrect answers to production queries.
key_works: Chu et al. (2018), *Axiomatic Foundations and Algorithms for Deciding Semantic Equivalences of SQL Queries*, DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200.

title: Verified query compilation through execution backends
open: Can a single compositional proof carry a query from its relational semantics all the way through executable query plans, code generation, runtime operators, and distributed execution? Formally, this asks for end-to-end verification linking each stage of a query compiler and its execution backends so that correctness composes across the whole pipeline.
status: Q*cert (Auerbach, Hirzel, Mandel, Shinnar, and Siméon, 2017, *Q*cert: A Platform for Implementing and Verifying Query Compilers*; the same authors, *Prototyping a Query Compiler Using Coq*) demonstrates verified query-compilation infrastructure, but broad backend and operational coverage remains an extension target.
solved_when: A verified query-compilation pipeline exists in which relational semantics are connected through query plans, code generation, runtime operators, and distributed execution by one compositional proof, with verified coverage across broadly varied backends and operational scenarios.
why: It closes the gap between a correct query rewrite and a correct query result: even a provably correct optimizer step guarantees nothing if compilation or execution can introduce errors downstream.
key_works: Auerbach, Hirzel, Mandel, Shinnar, and Siméon (2017), *Q*cert: A Platform for Implementing and Verifying Query Compilers*; the same authors, *Prototyping a Query Compiler Using Coq*.

title: Implementation proofs of weak isolation
open: Can a real database implementation be proved, end to end, to provide its advertised isolation level — including recovery, index maintenance, replication, and concurrent maintenance operations — rather than just an abstract concurrency-control core?
status: Weak-isolation logics such as that of Kapi et al. (2018), *Alone Together: Compositional Reasoning and Inference for Weak Isolation* (DOI:10.1145/3158115), support reasoning about transactions, and *Verifying Isolation Levels of Database Implementations* (2026, arXiv:2607.15877) advances implementation-level verification; the remaining gap is connecting operational mechanisms — recovery, indexes, replication, concurrent maintenance — to those semantics.
solved_when: A proof exists that covers a real database implementation at its advertised isolation level, with recovery, indexes, replication, and concurrent maintenance included in the verified scope.
why: It would make advertised consistency guarantees independently checkable, replacing trust in vendor claims with a machine-checkable artifact.
key_works: Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together: Compositional Reasoning and Inference for Weak Isolation*, DOI:10.1145/3158115; *Verifying Isolation Levels of Database Implementations* (2026), arXiv:2607.15877.

title: Minimal synchronization for application invariants
open: Can we automatically determine, for a given set of declared application invariants, the weakest isolation level or coordination scheme that still preserves them — with machine-checked reasoning covering all concurrent transactions?
status: Compositional weak-isolation reasoning (Kaki et al. 2018, *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115) and anomaly detection (*Automated Detection of Serializability Violations under Weak Consistency*, 2018, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2018.41) supply partial approaches; optimal coordination choices remain application- and model-dependent.
solved_when: A method exists that, given declared invariants, infers a minimal synchronization/coordination requirement and proves preservation under all concurrent transaction interleavings.
why: It lets systems shed synchronization that is not needed for correctness, trading unnecessary coordination for proved invariant preservation.
key_works: Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115; *Automated Detection of Serializability Violations under Weak Consistency* (2018), DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2018.41.

title: Verified online schema migration
open: Can we prove a database schema migration correct while the system keeps serving reads and writes throughout — including under mixed application versions, backfills, rollback, and interrupted execution?
status: The ingredients exist separately — query equivalence results, crash reasoning frameworks, and mixed-version protocols — but an integrated proof of the full migration process remains the target; relevant foundations include Chu et al. (2018), DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; and Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.
solved_when: A machine-checked correctness proof exists for an online schema migration protocol covering the full scenario set stated above: concurrent reads and writes, coexisting old and new application versions, backfill phases, rollback, and crash- or interruption-resilient execution.
why: Schema migration is one of the highest-risk maintenance operations on persistent data; a verified protocol would protect against data corruption or loss during live evolution of production storage systems.
key_works: Chu et al. (2018), DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Verified backup and restore semantics
open: Can we prove that a backup taken by a real system corresponds exactly to a declared consistency point, and that restoring it preserves the application's invariants — even in the presence of partial uploads, detected corruption, and format or version changes?
status: Crash-safe and distributed verification — e.g., Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*, and Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove* — establish relevant foundations, but backup correctness is not implied by local crash safety and remains unaddressed.
solved_when: A machine-checked (or otherwise rigorous) proof exists showing backup correspondence with declared consistency points and restoration-preservation of application invariants under partial uploads, corruption detection, and version changes.
why: It turns disaster recovery from an untested assumption into an assured capability, so a restore after failure provably reconstructes a valid system state.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Parameterized cache-coherence proofs with implementation detail
open: Can we formally verify a cache-coherence implementation so that the proof scales to any supported number of cores while still modeling the messy realities of real hardware — buffered messages, eviction, DMA, and heterogeneous agents?
status: Kami demonstrates parametric hardware verification, but richer industrial coherence envelopes remain a distinct target. Key work: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami: A Platform for High-Level Parametric Hardware Specification and Its Modular Verification*, DOI:10.1145/3110268.
solved_when: A machine-checked proof establishes coherence for arbitrary core counts over an implementation that includes realistic buffering, eviction, DMA, and heterogeneous agents.
why: It removes reliance on bounded small-core model checking, which cannot justify coherence on the large, heterogeneous systems actually shipped.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami: A Platform for High-Level Parametric Hardware Specification and Its Modular Verification*, DOI:10.1145/3110268.

title: Fault-tolerant adaptive network-on-chip verification
open: Can we formally verify that an adaptive network-on-chip keeps packets safe, deadlock-free, and making progress even when links or routers fail, with proofs that scale across parameterized topologies?
status: NoC-Out (Kurze, Farka, and Ertel, 2026, arXiv:2608.24478) verifies a multidimensional torus generator with strong liveness; adaptive fault-tolerant routing is a narrower extension, not an untouched field.
solved_when: A machine-checked proof establishes safety, deadlock freedom, and useful progress for adaptive routing under link/router failures, covering parameterized (not fixed-size) topologies.
why: It would give a trustworthy foundation for reliable communication fabrics in many-core chips, where unverified adaptive routing risks deadlock or message loss in the field.
key_works: Kurze, Farka, and Ertel (2026), *NoC-Out: A Formally-Verified Network-on-Chip Library for Rule-Based Hardware Designs*, arXiv:2608.24478.

title: Composable hardware/software speculation contracts
open: Can we design speculation contracts under which a software security proof carries over to any compliant speculative microarchitecture, without the proof having to model each implementation's details? Formally, the goal is a contract framework whose guarantees are portable and composable across multiple compliant implementations and modern speculative features.
status: SPECTECTOR (Guarnieri et al., 2020, *SPECTECTOR: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows*, arXiv:1812.08639) and the associated *Hardware/Software Contracts for Secure Speculation* line of work establish substantial partial approaches; portability and composition across modern speculative features remain open targets.
solved_when: A contract formalism exists for which software proofs of speculative noninterference remain valid across several compliant speculative microarchitectures, with composition and portability covering modern speculative features, without requiring modeling of every implementation detail.
why: It would make speculative-execution security guarantees reusable across hardware generations rather than re-proven per microarchitecture, and would enable portable mitigation of microarchitectural side channels in software.
key_works: Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows*, arXiv:1812.08639; associated *Hardware/Software Contracts for Secure Speculation* resources.

title: Physical leakage guarantees beyond constant-time timing models
open: Can we connect formal proofs at the register-transfer level, such as those establishing constant-time execution of hardware, to explicit models of power or electromagnetic leakage, and empirically determine where such models accurately bound the information an attacker can actually observe?
status: Iodine (von Gleissenthall et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.03111) verifies hardware constant-time properties, but constant-time execution does not itself prove absence of power or electromagnetic leakage; no validated connection between such proofs and physical leakage models yet exists.
solved_when: An RTL-level verified design is paired with an explicit power or electromagnetic leakage model, and validation demonstrates the conditions under which the model bounds observable leaked information.
why: It prevents timing proofs from being overinterpreted as complete side-channel security, since constant-time execution alone does not rule out power or electromagnetic leakage.
key_works: von Gleissenthall et al. (2019), *Iodine: Verifying Constant-Time Execution of Hardware*, arXiv:1910.03111.

title: Verified clock-domain and reset-domain integration
open: Can we formally verify multi-clock digital hardware designs in a way that explicitly models the asynchronous relationships between clock domains, reset sequencing, and metastability containment, rather than assuming them away? In other words, can correctness proofs of digital protocols be extended to cover these physical-level effects as first-class elements of the model?
status: Existing digital hardware frameworks (e.g., Kami, Choi et al. 2017, DOI:10.1145/3110268; ISA Semantics, Armstrong et al. 2019, DOI:10.1145/3290384) provide the logical foundations for hardware verification, but analog phenomena are not yet modeled; they must remain explicit assumptions or be tied to validated physical models.
solved_when: A verification framework exists in which digital protocols are proven correct with asynchronous clock relationships, reset sequencing, and metastability-containment assumptions explicitly modeled — with analog phenomena either kept as explicit, clearly stated assumptions or connected to validated physical models.
why: Ordinary synchronous RTL reasoning misses whole classes of failures — cross-domain synchronization faults, reset-ordering bugs, and metastability hazards — so designs that "verify" cleanly today can still fail in silicon.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

title: Proof-preserving hardware optimization and physical-design handoff
open: Can we carry a machine-checked equivalence proof all the way from a verified hardware description through every optimization, synthesis, and implementation transformation, under explicitly stated timing assumptions, so that the fabricated artifact is covered by the original proof?
status: High-level hardware proofs exist (e.g., Kami, Choi et al. 2017, DOI:10.1145/3110268), but they do not automatically cover every downstream tool transformation; work on end-to-end verified implementation flows is ongoing (Kurze et al. 2026, *NoC-Out*, arXiv:2608.24478).
solved_when: A verified hardware description can be passed through optimization, synthesis, and physical implementation with equivalence to the checked source maintained at each step under explicit timing assumptions, yielding a fabricated design provably corresponding to the verified description.
why: Without it, high-level hardware proofs do not automatically cover every downstream tool transformation, so the chip that is actually fabricated may not correspond to the description that was verified.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268; Kurze et al. (2026), *NoC-Out*, arXiv:2608.24478.

title: End-to-end verified post-quantum implementation suites
open: Can a full post-quantum cryptographic suite be verified end-to-end, from its mathematical operations down to optimized code, serialization, error handling, and the deployment platforms it targets?
status: EverCrypt and Fiat Cryptography demonstrate powerful verified-implementation techniques, but complete suite coverage must be established algorithm by algorithm; no end-to-end verified post-quantum suite yet exists.
solved_when: A declared post-quantum cryptographic suite carries machine-checked proofs covering the entire chain: mathematical specification, optimized implementation, serialization, error handling, and supported deployment platforms.
why: It removes implementation risk during the cryptographic migration to post-quantum algorithms, where a single unverified layer can undo the security of the whole suite.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider*; Erbsen et al. (2019), *Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic—With Proofs, Without Compromises*.

title: Constant-time preservation through complete compilation
open: Does a realistic compilation and linking pipeline preserve a precisely stated leakage property — not merely functional correctness — for cryptographic code? Formally, can constant-time behavior be shown to survive the full compiler and linker path, in the way that ordinary compiler correctness theorems do not deliver?
status: Verified cryptographic libraries and speculative-flow analyses provide the needed components — e.g., Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*, and Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR* (arXiv:1812.08639) — but ordinary compiler correctness does not imply leakage preservation, and no such preservation result for the full pipeline is in hand.
solved_when: A proof exists that the complete compilation and linking pipeline preserves the stated leakage property (e.g., constant-time / noninterference-style behavior) for cryptographic code, covering the optimizations along the path rather than functional behavior alone.
why: It prevents compiler optimizations from silently reintroducing secret-dependent behavior in code that was verified constant-time at the source level.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*, arXiv:1812.08639.

title: Verified masked implementations under realistic leakage models
open: Can we build implementations of masking that carry machine-checked proofs of both functional correctness and security against leakage, where the leakage model reflects physical reality — glitches, transition effects, randomness reuse, and the transformations a compiler may apply — rather than an idealized wire-value model?
status: Existing constant-time verification and verified arithmetic work (e.g., Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt*) supplies only part of this assurance; verifying masking requires richer leakage reasoning, as explored by von Gleissenthall et al. (2019), *Iodine* (arXiv:1910.03111).
solved_when: A framework and verified implementation exist that prove correctness and masking security under a leakage model explicitly accounting for glitches, transitions, randomness reuse, and compiler transformations.
why: Constant-time code does not exclude physical leakage such as power side channels; masking is the main defense, and without proofs under realistic leakage models, verified implementations can still fall to attacks the model ignored.
key_works: von Gleissenthall et al. (2019), *Iodine*, arXiv:1910.03111; Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*.

title: Verified cryptographic fault defenses
open: Can we prove that a cryptographic implementation detects, or safely handles, every fault in a declared class of injected faults — including faults that alter control flow, security checks, and outputs?
status: Functional correctness proofs generally assume fault-free execution; hardware and cryptographic verification, including works such as Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*, and Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, provide foundations for explicit fault extensions. Realistic and compositional fault-injection models in hardware security remain a related open direction.
solved_when: A verified implementation exists for which machine-checked proofs show detection or safe handling of all faults in the declared class (control flow, checks, and outputs).
why: Physical fault attacks bypass functional correctness guarantees by corrupting execution at runtime, so high-value cryptographic operations need defenses whose safety holds under faults, not just in fault-free execution.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*.

title: Proven cryptographic agility without downgrade paths
open: Can we formally verify a cryptographic stack's agility mechanisms — protocol negotiation, algorithm replacement, fallback, and configuration changes — so that no sequence of choices can silently weaken the required security level?
status: EverCrypt (Protzenko et al., 2020) proves important agility mechanisms, but whole-protocol negotiation and operational configuration enlarge the target; the Tamarin prover and its protocol-analysis case studies provide relevant tooling for protocol-level reasoning.
solved_when: A verified implementation exists in which negotiation, replacement, fallback, and configuration changes are all covered by machine-checked proofs guaranteeing that the security level required by policy is never downgraded through any agility path.
why: It makes migration capability compatible with stable security guarantees, so that upgrading or reconfiguring cryptography cannot become an attack surface.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Tamarin prover, protocol-analysis documentation and case studies.

bib.title: Proven cryptographic agility without downgrade paths

title: Verified entropy acquisition and random-number lifecycle
open: Can we formally connect a cryptosystem's probabilistic security proof to the full operational lifecycle of its randomness source — covering entropy acquisition, seeding, reseeding, state compromise, process cloning, and restart behavior?
status: Mathematical cryptographic proofs and verified implementations (e.g., Project Everest, project documentation; Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*) frequently expose unproven randomness assumptions; discharging the operational lifecycle remains an open engineering target. A related direction is validated entropy estimation under adversarial conditions from information theory.
solved_when: A verified implementation exists in which the probabilistic security proof's randomness assumptions are discharged end-to-end across the random-number lifecycle: entropy acquisition, seeding, reseeding, state compromise, process cloning, and restart behavior.
why: It prevents cryptographically correct algorithms from failing in practice because their randomness assumptions turn out to be false in deployment.
key_works: Project Everest, project documentation; Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*.

bib.title: Verified entropy acquisition and random-number lifecycle

title: Automated verified arithmetic generation beyond prime-field kernels
open: Can automated synthesis produce machine-verified, competitive arithmetic code beyond prime-field kernels — for richer algebraic structures, longer operation sequences, and architecture-specific optimizations?
status: Fiat Cryptography (Erbsen, Philipoom, Gross, Sloan, and Chlipala, 2019, *Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic—With Proofs, Without Compromises*) demonstrates that generated arithmetic can be both proved and fast; broader algebraic and backend coverage remains the target.
solved_when: A verified-code-generation pipeline covers these broader algebraic structures and operation sequences, produces architecture-specific optimized output, and the generated code is both proved correct and competitive in performance with hand-written implementations.
why: It removes the need for hand-written low-level arithmetic, along with the error-prone audit burden that such code carries.
key_works: Erbsen, Philipoom, Gross, Sloan, and Chlipala (2019), *Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic—With Proofs, Without Compromises*.

title: Symbolic-to-computational security with implementation alignment
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can a symbolic proof of a security protocol be extended into a full computational and implementation-level guarantee, covering the actual wire encoding and the behavior of real cryptographic APIs? In other words, when does a symbolic argument correspond to concrete security for the deployed implementation rather than only an idealized model?
status: The Tamarin prover analyzes substantial real protocols, with case studies published on TLS, 5G, Noise, EMV, and messaging, and Project Everest pursues verified implementations; however, a symbolic proof does not automatically supply every computational and implementation correspondence.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a symbolic protocol proof, mechanically yields the corresponding computational security statement together with the alignment to the implementation's encoding and cryptographic API behavior — so that a symbolic proof automatically supplies every computational and implementation correspondence.
why: Without it, verified protocols can still be insecure at the level that actually runs; with it, protocol assurance becomes meaningful across abstraction layers rather than confined to the symbolic model.
key_works: Tamarin prover, documentation and published TLS, 5G, Noise, EMV, and messaging case studies; Project Everest.

title: Scalable protocol proof under key compromise and recovery
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can a long-running deployed protocol be formally verified across its entire key lifecycle — compromise, rotation, device replacement, and recovery — with explicit, stated guarantees for each phase rather than a single monolithic security claim?
status: Modern protocol analyses, including Tamarin prover case studies of modern messaging and security protocols, already cover rich security properties; the combined lifecycle and state-space burden remains a scoped scaling target.
solved_when: A machine-checked proof exists for a long-running protocol covering repeated compromise, key rotation, device replacement, and recovery, with per-phase guarantees made explicit and the combined lifecycle state space handled at scale.
why: It models security over years of real operation rather than one clean session, which is the regime in which deployed protocols actually fail.
key_works: Tamarin prover and its modern messaging/security-protocol case studies.

title: Authorization proofs across identity and application boundaries
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can one prove that a real-world identity stack — tokens, sessions, delegated credentials, revocation, and application-level permissions — composed across service boundaries enforces exactly the one intended authorization policy? In other words, is end-to-end authorization across identity and application boundaries a tractable formal-verification target?
status: Protocol-analysis tools (e.g., the Tamarin prover) and verified-system techniques provide the ingredients, but operational identity composition across services remains a separate, unaddressed assurance target; no such composition proof currently exists.
solved_when: A machine-checkable proof exists that the composed system (tokens, sessions, delegation, revocation, and application permissions, across services) enforces the single intended authorization policy, with no confused-deputy or stale-authorization behaviors.
why: It prevents confused-deputy and stale-authorization failures, which are exactly the class of bugs that arise when identity and application layers each look correct in isolation but compose into unintended access.
key_works: Tamarin prover documentation; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Noninterference with explicit declassification budgets
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: How can we verify systems that intentionally release selected information while proving that all other flows remain bounded by a precise, quantitative policy?
status: Hyperproperty and leakage-verification frameworks provide foundations, including *HyperProb* (2021), DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-90870-6_35, and Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*. Practical policy composition and quantitative declassification remain challenging.
solved_when: A verification method exists that, for a system with an explicit declassification budget, proves noninterference for all flows except those permitted by the policy and bounds the released information within the stated budget.
why: It replaces unrealistic "release nothing" policies with useful security guarantees, allowing systems to be both functional and provably secure.
key_works: *HyperProb* (2021), DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-90870-6_35; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*.

title: Automatic coupling discovery for privacy proofs
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can a system automatically discover probabilistic couplings for differential-privacy proofs, going beyond verification against fixed, hand-designed coupling templates — and independently check the couplings it finds?
status: Coupling-based logics already verify important mechanisms, including analyses not captured by simple composition alone (Barthe, Gaboardi, Grégoire, Hsu, and Strub, 2016, *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*, arXiv:1601.05047, DOI:10.1145/2933575.2934554); what is missing is automatic construction of the couplings themselves.
solved_when: A tool takes privacy mechanisms (including ones whose analyses are not captured by simple composition alone) and synthesizes couplings automatically, with independent machine-checkable verification of each discovered coupling, without relying on a fixed template library.
why: It would remove the specialized mathematical effort currently needed to design couplings by hand, making differential-privacy verification far more accessible and scalable.
key_works: Barthe, Gaboardi, Grégoire, Hsu, and Strub (2016), *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*, arXiv:1601.05047, DOI:10.1145/2933575.2934554.

title: Verified adaptive privacy accounting
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can we build a verified system that correctly accounts for a privacy budget even when queries, stopping rules, and mechanisms are chosen adaptively at runtime? Formally, this means tracking budget consumption through persistent state and across crash-recovery events, so the accounting itself is machine-checked rather than assumed.
status: Relational probabilistic logics establish important privacy foundations (e.g., Barthe et al. 2016, *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*), and verified-systems infrastructure such as Perennial (Chajed et al. 2019) supports stateful verification. What remains open is that stateful operational accounting adds software and lifecycle obligations these foundations do not yet cover; related statistical work on adaptive composition and privacy filters addresses the analytic side.
solved_when: A verified accounting system exists that soundly tracks privacy-budget consumption under adaptively chosen queries, stopping rules, and mechanisms, maintains correct accounting through persistent state, and recovers correctly from crashes without losing or double-counting budget.
why: It prevents a correct mechanism from being overused by an incorrect service — a sound analysis of a DP mechanism is worthless if the surrounding service can spend more budget than the analysis certifies.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*.

title: Privacy proofs across distributed data pipelines
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Can we prove end-to-end privacy for a distributed data pipeline, so the guarantee attached to the delivered data product is justified by what every stage actually did? Concretely, this means composing privacy proofs across ingestion, joins, contribution bounding, private aggregation, caching, and output publication, all under explicit trust boundaries.
status: Existing work on mechanism-level privacy and query-compilation verification (e.g., Barthe et al., 2016, arXiv:1601.05047; Auerbach et al., 2017, *Q*cert) provides foundations, but pipeline semantics can invalidate the assumptions these mechanism-level proofs rely on.
solved_when: A verification framework exists that composes mechanism-level and query-compilation proofs across all pipeline stages — ingestion, joins, contribution bounding, private aggregation, caching, and output publication — and yields an end-to-end guarantee for the delivered data product under stated trust boundaries.
why: Without pipeline-level composition, a mechanism's privacy guarantee can be invalidated by the semantics of the stages surrounding it, so the delivered data product may carry no real guarantee at all.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), arXiv:1601.05047; Auerbach et al. (2017), *Q*cert*.

bib.title: Privacy proofs across distributed data pipelines

title: Certified elementary-function implementations across full domains
open: Can we build production-grade elementary-function libraries whose accuracy and exceptional behavior are formally certified over their entire input domains? Concretely, this means verifying every supported input, rounding mode, and implementation branch of the optimized code that actually ships.
status: Dandelion (2022, arXiv:2202.05472) certifies approximations of elementary functions, building on techniques such as Becker et al. (2018, arXiv:1707.02115); connecting these approximation proofs to complete optimized library implementations remains open.
solved_when: A complete optimized library implementation of the elementary functions is accompanied by a machine-checked proof covering accuracy and exceptional behavior for all supported inputs, all rounding modes, and all implementation branches.
why: It eliminates a pervasive trusted numerical component that nearly every scientific and systems program silently relies on.
key_works: *Dandelion: Certified Approximations of Elementary Functions* (2022), arXiv:2202.05472; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Verified mixed-precision optimization
open: Can a tool automatically select floating-point precisions and program transformations that provably meet a stated error tolerance while simultaneously optimizing measured execution cost on the target hardware?
status: Verified certificate checking for finite-precision error bounds (Becker et al. 2018, *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, DOI:10.23919/FMCAD.2018.8603019) provides a foundation, but joint optimization of precision, control flow, and hardware performance remains the target.
solved_when: A system exists that, given a program and error tolerance, jointly optimizes precision, control flow, and hardware performance, producing a certified mixed-precision configuration whose error bound is formally verified and whose cost is improved on the target platform.
why: It would deliver speed and energy savings without sacrificing the stated numerical accuracy, closing the gap between verified error bounds and real hardware performance.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, DOI:10.23919/FMCAD.2018.8603019.

title: Verified parallel reductions with reproducibility guarantees
open: Can we build a verified parallel reduction whose floating-point result is guaranteed reproducible even as thread counts, schedulings, and vectorization choices change? Formally, this asks for machine-checked numerical bounds and reproducibility properties for parallel reductions under nonassociative floating-point arithmetic across all these execution variations.
status: Existing work supplies components: arithmetic verification (Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115) and concurrency semantics (Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*). What remains hard is composition: floating-point operations are nonassociative, so reordering work in a parallel reduction changes the result, and no existing combination of these components closes that gap.
solved_when: A verified implementation of parallel reduction exists with proved numerical error bounds and proved reproducibility — i.e., identical results for any thread count, scheduling, or vectorization configuration.
why: It would make large-scale scientific and machine-learning computations produce bit-identical results across runs and platforms, turning reproducibility from an empirical hope into a guarantee.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*.

title: Certified iterative solver termination and accuracy
open: When an iterative numerical solver halts on real hardware, can we formally certify that its stopping decision and accuracy claims are sound despite floating-point roundoff, ill-conditioning, and finite resource limits — including soundly reporting when it cannot guarantee accuracy? A second sentence may formalize this as: give a machine-checkable justification, or a justified failure report, for the stopping test actually executed by the solver.
status: Certified numerical reasoning exists (e.g., Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Gao et al., dReal research publications), but convergence theorems proved over exact arithmetic do not automatically justify the executable stopping tests used in practice, leaving the gap between theory and machine-level termination decisions open.
solved_when: A method exists that, for an iterative solver run in finite-precision arithmetic on ill-conditioned problems under bounded resources, produces a formal certificate that the stopping criterion's accuracy claims are valid, or a justified report that certification failed — replacing silent acceptance of unreliable results with either certified accuracy or an explicit failure declaration.
why: Without it, solvers may silently accept inaccurate numerical solutions, with the errors masked by roundoff and ill-conditioning rather than reported to the user.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Gao et al., dReal research publications.
