title: End-to-end verified scientific simulation pipelines
open: Can we build a scientific simulation pipeline in which discretization error, numerical error, solver behavior, and implementation correctness are connected in a single verified chain for a declared simulation task — with the framework able to distinguish modeling error from software error end to end?
status: Formal numerical and hybrid-system tools address pieces of the chain; no existing approach connects the full chain or distinguishes modeling error from software error throughout. Key works include Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115, and Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-21401-6_36.
solved_when: A declared simulation task is supported by a verification pipeline that formally connects discretization error, numerical error, solver behavior, and implementation correctness, and cleanly separates modeling error from software error across the full chain.
why: It gives scientific conclusions an explicit computational assurance boundary, so users know exactly which errors have been bounded and which remain unverified.

bib.title: End-to-end verified scientific simulation pipelines

title: Numerical proof transfer to optimized machine code
open: Can a numerical error bound proved for source-level code be carried through to the compiled, optimized binary — surviving compiler rewrites, fused operations, vectorization, and substitution of library routines — with a formal guarantee of the resulting quantitative error? Formally, this asks for a refinement framework in which quantitative semantic properties, not just functional correctness, are preserved by each transformation in the compilation pipeline.
status: Verified compilation and numerical certificates are established as separate lines of work (Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030), but preserving quantitative error contracts is stronger than ordinary functional refinement and remains open.
solved_when: A verified compilation pipeline (or equivalent proof-transfer method) exists that, given a proved floating-point error bound at the source level, produces a machine-checked bound on the optimized executable produced by the pipeline, covering the transformation classes named (compiler rewrites, fusion, vectorization, library substitution).
why: Without it, a numerical proof about source code says nothing about the deployed optimized binary, so certified scientific software silently loses its guarantees the moment optimization is switched on; with it, source-level numerical proofs remain valid in optimized deployments.

bib.title: Numerical proof transfer to optimized machine code

title: Verified sampled-data implementation of continuous controllers
open: When a continuous controller is implemented as a sampled program running on real hardware, does the implementation still satisfy the guarantees proved for the ideal controller — despite finite-precision arithmetic, execution delay, and bounded scheduling jitter?
status: Hybrid-system reasoning and numerical verification provide the needed components; ideal continuous proofs alone do not establish implementation safety. Key works include Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*, and Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.
solved_when: A verification method exists that, given a continuous controller and its guarantees, produces a machine-checked proof that a sampled, finite-precision implementation with execution delay and bounded scheduling jitter preserves those guarantees.
why: It closes the gap between controller mathematics and embedded execution, so that safety proofs transfer from the design model to the code actually running on the vehicle or robot.
key_works: Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

bib.title: Verified sampled-data implementation of continuous controllers

title: Compositional safety for interacting hybrid components
open: Can we find local safety contracts for interacting hybrid components such that composing them proves the global system safe, even when components are coupled through feedback, shared resources, and continuous dynamics? Formally, the challenge is a contract framework whose composition rule is sound for closed hybrid systems with interdependent continuous state.
status: Hybrid proof systems are expressive — Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1, and Mitsch and Platzer (2017), *The KeYmaera X Proof IDE*, arXiv:1701.08469 — but useful automatic contract discovery and scalable composition remain separate, unreached targets.
solved_when: A method exists that, given interacting hybrid components, derives local contracts and a composition rule that together yield a proof of global safety in the presence of feedback, shared resources, and coupled continuous dynamics.
why: It removes the need for monolithic proofs of complex cyber-physical systems, which do not scale as component count and interaction grow.
key_works: Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; Mitsch and Platzer (2017), *The KeYmaera X Proof IDE*, arXiv:1701.08469.

bib.title: Compositional safety for interacting hybrid components

title: Formal treatment of contact, impacts, and mode explosion
open: Can we formally verify robotic and mechanical systems whose dynamics include contact changes, impacts, and friction, using explicit physical abstractions and while keeping the combinatorial explosion of contact modes under control?
status: Hybrid verification provides a framework, but realistic contact dynamics and model uncertainty create additional difficulties. Tools in this tradition include KeYmaera X (Fulton et al., 2015) and dReal with satisfiability-modulo-ODE methods (Gao et al.).
solved_when: A verification method exists that handles contact-rich dynamics with impacts and friction under explicit physical abstractions and gives formal guarantees without the number of hybrid modes exploding combinatorially.
why: It would extend formal guarantees to manipulation and locomotion, where contact-rich behavior under uncertain mechanics is the norm rather than the exception.
key_works: Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*; Gao et al., dReal and satisfiability-modulo-ODE publications.

bib.title: Formal treatment of contact, impacts, and mode explosion

title: Verified prevention of Zeno behavior in synthesized controllers
open: Can we automatically synthesize, or repair, hybrid controllers that provably never exhibit Zeno behavior — infinitely many discrete transitions in finite time — while still meeting their safety objectives?
status: Hybrid logics can express the relevant reasoning, but the automatic construction of useful non-Zeno guarantees remains an open target. Key works include Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1, and the KeYmaera X documentation.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a hybrid controller, produces or repairs it together with a machine-checked proof excluding infinitely many discrete transitions in finite time, with all original safety objectives retained.
why: It guarantees that mathematically synthesized controllers correspond to behavior that is physically executable, rather than artifacts of an idealized model that no real system can follow.
key_works: Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; KeYmaera X documentation.

bib.title: Verified prevention of Zeno behavior in synthesized controllers

title: Safe learning of dynamics with explicit model-validity regions
open: Can a learning-based controller learn the dynamics of a system while simultaneously maintaining an explicit, certified region in which the learned model's error bounds are tight enough to justify the controller's safety guarantees?
status: Verified-AI and hybrid verification research identifies model uncertainty as central; see Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514. Related work on system identification provides finite-data guarantees for nonlinear dynamics.
solved_when: A method demonstrably learns a dynamics model together with certified model-validity regions in which the model's error bounds suffice to guarantee the controller's safety, verified experimentally.
why: It makes learning-based control compatible with defensible safety guarantees, replacing sampled prediction accuracy — which is not a safety certificate — with regions where guarantees provably hold.
key_works: Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

bib.title: Safe learning of dynamics with explicit model-validity regions

title: Verifiable recovery controllers under actuator degradation
open: Can we design and formally verify a recovery controller that keeps a system safe when its sensors or actuators degrade, so that safety holds even while the fault is being detected and control is switching over? The goal is a controller with machine-checked safety guarantees under explicitly modeled failure sets, accounting for detection delay and switching dynamics.
status: Hybrid proof tools such as KeYmaera X already support safety reasoning for hybrid systems, but combining fault diagnosis, degraded dynamics, and implementation timing into a single verified recovery controller remains the proposed target; related challenges are surveyed in Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, arXiv:1811.06740.
solved_when: A recovery controller is constructed whose safe fallback behavior under sensor or actuator degradation within explicitly modeled failure sets is formally proven, with the proof covering detection delay and switching behavior.
why: It preserves safety precisely when the assumptions underlying the normal controller stop holding, closing the gap between fault-tolerant control and machine-checked verification for degraded-operation scenarios.
key_works: KeYmaera X publications; Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, arXiv:1811.06740.

bib.title: Verifiable recovery controllers under actuator degradation

title: Proof-producing high-dimensional reachability
open: Can conservative reachability analysis be scaled to high-dimensional nonlinear systems while producing certificates that an independent checker can verify without trusting the numerical reachability engine?
status: δ-complete solvers and hybrid theorem provers provide complementary baselines (Gao et al., dReal publications; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*); dimension and nonlinearity remain substantial scaling barriers.
solved_when: A tool computes reachability for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and exports independently checkable certificates, with scalability beyond the barriers currently posed by dimension and nonlinearity.
why: It would make large cyber-physical safety analyses independently auditable rather than dependent on trust in a single numerical engine.
key_works: Gao et al., dReal publications; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

bib.title: Proof-producing high-dimensional reachability

title: Sound monitoring with missing and reordered events
open: How should a runtime monitor interpret an event stream in which observations may be dropped, duplicated, delayed, or reordered, and what verdict semantics should it adopt so that it reports justified uncertainty rather than false certainty about the system under observation?
status: Distributed and advanced-domain runtime verification recognizes observation quality as a core challenge (Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, DOI:10.1007/s10703-019-00337-w, arXiv:1811.06740); reasoning from incomplete event histories is a recognized concern in distributed systems.
solved_when: A monitor semantics is given that explicitly accounts for dropped, duplicated, delayed, and reordered observations and yields verdicts expressing uncertainty justified by the quality of the observation stream, rather than definite verdicts that can be wrong.
why: It would make runtime-monitoring guarantees robust to the behavior of real telemetry pipelines, where imperfect observation is the norm, instead of relying on assumptions that pipelines rarely satisfy.
key_works: Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, DOI:10.1007/s10703-019-00337-w, arXiv:1811.06740.

bib.title: Sound monitoring with missing and reordered events

title: Verified instrumentation with bounded observer effects
open: Can we build instrumentation that provably observes everything a monitor needs to see while leaving the monitored system's relevant behavior intact? Formally, this asks for a verified observation mechanism whose effect on the target is bounded by explicit timing and resource budgets.
status: Runtime monitoring depends on an observation mechanism, and its correctness and perturbation cost are separate concerns from the monitor's logical correctness; this separation is currently unaddressed. Related work includes Sánchez et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.06740, and Ringer et al. (2020), *REPLICA: REPL Instrumentation for Coq Analysis*.
solved_when: A proof exists that the instrumentation captures all required events, preserves the relevant behaviors of the instrumented system, and stays within the stated timing and resource budgets.
why: It prevents the monitoring system from invalidating the very assumptions it is meant to check — an unverified or overly intrusive observer can silently break the properties under observation.
key_works: Sánchez et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.06740; Ringer et al. (2020), *REPLICA: REPL Instrumentation for Coq Analysis*.

bib.title: Verified instrumentation with bounded observer effects

title: Distributed monitoring with optimal communication
open: How much communication is actually necessary for a set of distributed processes to jointly monitor a temporal property at runtime? The goal is to establish matching lower and upper bounds for communication cost when monitoring chosen temporal properties under explicit models of clocks and failures.
status: Distributed runtime verification is established, but tight property-dependent communication trade-offs remain an open theory frontier; related work includes communication complexity of distributed evaluation of temporal predicates (Sánchez et al. 2019, DOI:10.1007/s10703-019-00337-w).
solved_when: For selected temporal properties, tight communication lower bounds are proven under an explicitly specified clock and failure model, together with monitors whose communication cost matches those bounds.
why: Tight bounds tell designers of constrained networks exactly how much bandwidth monitoring requires, making runtime verification feasible where communication is the scarce resource.

bib.title: Distributed monitoring with optimal communication

title: Minimal-intervention enforcement with hard deadlines
open: Can we synthesize a runtime enforcer for a temporal policy that alters the system's behavior as little as possible, while guaranteeing that the enforcer itself always responds within hard real-time deadlines?
status: Timed runtime enforcement is established, including time-retardant constructions (Pinisetty et al. 2012, *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23), and recent work enforces CPS against Signal Temporal Logic (*Runtime Enforcement of CPS against Signal Temporal Logic*, 2025, DOI:10.1145/3716863.3718052). Hard real-time minimal intervention, however, remains a stricter, unsolved target.
solved_when: A synthesis method exists that, given a timed temporal policy, produces an enforcer satisfying the policy, provably minimal in its interventions, and with a proof that every intervention meets the hard deadline bound.
why: Without it, enforcement of safety properties risks degrading the system to the point of unusability; minimal intervention preserves system utility while the deadline guarantee keeps the enforcer sound in real-time settings.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23; *Runtime Enforcement of CPS against Signal Temporal Logic* (2025), DOI:10.1145/3716863.3718052.

bib.title: Minimal-intervention enforcement with hard deadlines

title: Runtime enforcement of relational properties
open: Can a runtime enforcer police properties that relate multiple executions or users — such as information-flow and cross-session policies — without keeping unbounded history and without needlessly blocking behaviors that violate nothing? Formally, the goal is an enforcement mechanism for useful hyperproperties whose memory and its interference with benign traces are both bounded and justified.
status: Gray-box hyperproperty enforcement is an active research direction; ordinary single-trace safety monitoring does not settle it. Hsu et al. (2025), *Gray-Box Runtime Enforcement of Hyperproperties*, Acta Informatica paper, is a key work.
solved_when: A gray-box enforcement scheme exists that enforces meaningful hyperproperties over multiple executions while retaining only bounded history and provably restricting benign behavior no more than necessary for the target property.
why: It would bring runtime enforcement to relational policies like noninterference and cross-session security constraints, which single-trace safety monitors fundamentally cannot handle.
key_works: Hsu et al. (2025), *Gray-Box Runtime Enforcement of Hyperproperties*, Acta Informatica paper.

bib.title: Runtime enforcement of relational properties

title: Correct monitor evolution during live operation
open: How can a running monitor's policy or implementation be upgraded live without corrupting the meaning of its accumulated state or opening windows where enforcement lapses or duplicates?
status: Stateful monitors and proof-maintenance techniques (e.g., Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*) supply the ingredients; live semantic migration of monitors remains an open additional target.
solved_when: A live update mechanism exists that evolves a stateful monitor — policy and implementation — while preserving accumulated-state semantics and guaranteeing neither enforcement gaps nor duplicate enforcement throughout the transition.
why: It lets enforcement policies evolve without temporarily losing assurance on the system under protection.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

bib.title: Correct monitor evolution during live operation

title: Runtime verification of inferred vehicle behavior
open: Do inferred behavioral models of vehicle systems capture all legitimate operating modes while still flagging meaningful attacks — that is, can runtime verification distinguish genuinely anomalous behavior from benign behavior that was simply never observed during inference?
status: Desai et al. (2025) demonstrate stateful behavior inference and runtime enforcement for vehicle networks (*Stateful Behavior Inference and Runtime Enforcement for Vehicle Network Security*, USENIX VehicleSec); stronger coverage and generalization guarantees remain open targets.
solved_when: A validated inference-and-monitoring pipeline exists that both covers the relevant legitimate behavioral modes of the vehicle network and detects meaningful attacks, without classifying unseen benign behavior as a violation.
why: It connects formal runtime monitoring to systems whose behavior is only partially documented, so correctness no longer depends on having a complete manual specification.
key_works: Desai et al. (2025), *Stateful Behavior Inference and Runtime Enforcement for Vehicle Network Security*, USENIX VehicleSec.

bib.title: Runtime verification of inferred vehicle behavior

title: Proof-carrying runtime monitors
open: Can we automatically synthesize a runtime monitor that ships not only as executable code but as a verified artifact — carrying machine-checkable proofs of its semantic correctness, its instrumentation assumptions, its memory bounds, and its worst-case execution cost?
status: The necessary components exist separately — monitor synthesis, timed enforcement, and verified compilation (e.g., the CakeML project; Pinisetty et al., 2012, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23) — but packaging them into a complete assurance chain remains the target.
solved_when: A synthesis tool produces, for a given specification, an executable monitor together with proofs of semantic correctness, instrumentation assumptions, memory bounds, and worst-case execution cost, packaged as a complete assurance chain.
why: It makes runtime monitoring deployable in systems that cannot afford to trust a large unchecked enforcement stack, by replacing that trust with verified evidence.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23; CakeML project.

bib.title: Proof-carrying runtime monitors

title: Complete verification of large transformer components
open: Can we fully verify declared properties — robustness, safety, or other specified behaviors — of transformer blocks that include attention, normalization, and nonlinearities under realistic numerical semantics, at scales far beyond what current tools handle?
status: Neural verification competitions, summarized by Kaulen et al. (2025), *The 6th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition: Summary and Results*, arXiv:2512.19007, demonstrate progress on diverse models (see also VNN-COMP 2026 resources); architectural and scale coverage remain central frontiers.
solved_when: A verification method exists that proves declared properties for transformer components combining attention, normalization, and nonlinearities with realistic floating-point semantics at substantially larger scales than demonstrated by current neural verification competitions.
why: It extends formal assurance beyond small or specially structured networks, opening the path to certified reliability for the architectures actually deployed in practice.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), *The 6th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition: Summary and Results*, arXiv:2512.19007; VNN-COMP 2026 resources.

bib.title: Complete verification of large transformer components

title: Deployment-faithful neural-network certificates
open: Does a verified neural network remain verified once it is deployed — that is, can a certificate proved about the network be shown to apply to the actual quantized, optimized executable that runs in production, including kernels, rounding behavior, graph rewrites, and preprocessing? Formally, the goal is to construct a proof (or proof-carrying pipeline) that the deployed artifact refines the certified specification.
status: Network-level verification and numerical/compiler verification currently provide separate pieces of the picture; a mathematical certificate for the network does not automatically cover its deployment pipeline (Kaulen et al. 2025, arXiv:2512.19007; Becker et al. 2018, arXiv:1707.02115; Lopes et al. 2021, *Alive2*).
solved_when: A certificate established for the network is shown to transfer to the deployed executable end-to-end, covering quantization, compiler optimization, kernels, rounding, graph rewrites, and preprocessing — with no gap between the verified model and the running artifact.
why: Without it, a proof about the model says nothing about the code that actually executes, so the certificate guarantees only the artifact that was verified, not the system that ships; a solution closes this proof/model mismatch.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*.

bib.title: Deployment-faithful neural-network certificates

title: Semantic perturbation specifications
open: Can we define perturbation sets that capture meaningful real-world changes — changes a human would recognize as semantically relevant — rather than defaulting to convenient numerical norm balls? In formal terms, the goal is to construct and validate specification classes for semantic variation that neural-network verification tools can certify against.
status: Verified-AI research, notably Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence* (arXiv:1606.08514), identifies specification and environment modeling as central open problems; the community recognizes that better solvers cannot compensate for irrelevant property definitions. Related work in computer vision pursues formal models of semantic variation, but no validated semantic perturbation specification yet exists.
solved_when: A principled definition of a semantic perturbation set is given, validated experimentally on real-world variation models, and shown to be usable with existing verification machinery — so that certified robustness holds under perturbations that are semantically meaningful rather than norm-bounded alone.
why: Without semantic specifications, robustness certificates certify properties no user cares about; with them, verified-AI guarantees become useful outside benchmark abstractions.
key_works: Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

bib.title: Semantic perturbation specifications

title: Relational verification of learned models
open: Can we build verification tools that scale to properties relating a network's outputs across different inputs, groups of inputs, model versions, or execution conditions — with precise quantifiers and deployment semantics — rather than checking each input in isolation?
status: Relational and hyperproperty benchmark efforts already exist, so the target is broader coverage and scalable certified solving, not the first such benchmark. Key works include VNN-COMP 2025 relational benchmark discussions, *HyperProb* (2021), and Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007.
solved_when: A verification method and benchmark coverage exist that handle relational properties broadly (across inputs, groups, model versions, and execution conditions) with scalable certified solving, going beyond existing relational and hyperproperty benchmarks in coverage.
why: It directly underwrites consistency, fairness, and model-update guarantees for deployed learned models, which per-input verification cannot express.
key_works: VNN-COMP 2025 relational benchmark discussions; *HyperProb* (2021); Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007.

bib.title: Relational verification of learned models

title: Closed-loop verification with neural perception
open: Can we prove that an autonomous system is safe end-to-end when a neural network provides its perception and a controller acts on that perception? A satisfactory proof must account for uncertainty, timing, and temporal correlation in the perception component's errors.
status: The neural-network verification and hybrid-systems verification literatures each supply relevant methods, but robustness results for an isolated network do not transfer to closed-loop guarantees. Key works include Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514, and Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.
solved_when: A verification method exists that establishes system-level safety for a closed loop composed of a neural perception component feeding a controller, explicitly reasoning about uncertainty, timing, and temporal correlation in perception errors, rather than only the isolated network's robustness.
why: Without it, proofs of the perception network alone cannot certify the vehicle or robot it drives, since robustness of a component does not imply closed-loop safety; with it, verification targets the actual behavior of deployed autonomous systems.
key_works: Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

title: Certified robustness under model updates
open: When a neural network is fine-tuned, pruned, quantized, or architecturally modified, which previously certified input regions and properties provably survive the change? The goal is to develop transfer or repair guarantees that carry verification evidence across model updates rather than re-verifying from scratch.
status: Existing verification tools provide one-model baselines; efficient longitudinal certificate reuse remains a distinct, unachieved target. Related work includes Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007, and Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*; continual learning's concern with preserving previously guaranteed behavior is a related thread.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a certificate for a model and an update (fine-tuning, pruning, quantization, or architecture change), proves exactly which input regions and properties remain covered — and does so more efficiently than full re-verification, enabling certificate reuse across successive versions.
why: It would make formal verification compatible with continuously updated models, where re-running one-model verification tools after every change is the current barrier to maintaining guarantees in production.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Independently checkable neural verification certificates
open: Can the field agree on a standard format for certificates that lets a third party independently confirm a neural-network verification result, regardless of which solver family produced it? Such a standard must capture not only the final answer but also numerical soundness arguments and the provenance of any preprocessing applied to the network before verification.
status: VNN-COMP provides shared evaluation infrastructure for neural-network verification tools, but interoperable independent certificates remain an additional assurance objective beyond it; related effort exists on certificates for large nonconvex verification problems (Brix et al. 2023, DOI:10.1007/s10009-023-00703-4; Becker et al. 2018, arXiv:1707.02115).
solved_when: A compact certificate format is specified and adopted across solver families, such that checking a certificate — including its numerical reasoning and preprocessing provenance — requires no trust in the verifier's internal optimization or floating-point components.
why: Without independently checkable certificates, users must trust every numerical and optimization component of a large verifier, so a single bug anywhere in the toolchain can silently invalidate a claimed verification result.
key_works: Brix et al. (2023), *First Three Years of the International Verification of Neural Networks Competition*, DOI:10.1007/s10009-023-00703-4; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Formal authority boundaries for delegated agents
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can we give a precise formal semantics for delegation among LLM agents so that permissions, data access, budgets, and approval requirements propagate exactly as intended — with a proof that no delegation chain accidentally amplifies privilege beyond what the original principal granted?
status: Runtime policy systems provide a baseline for enforcing constraints on agents, but multi-agent authority composition still lacks explicit semantics; tools such as AgentSpec (Wang et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.18666) and the Tamarin prover's authorization-protocol modeling facilities offer building blocks for a formal treatment.
solved_when: A specification of authority propagation through delegation exists, together with a machine-checked or rigorous formal proof that composing delegated agents preserves the principal's constraints (no privilege amplification, no bypass of budgets or approval requirements) across arbitrary delegation chains.
why: Without such boundaries, a delegated subagent can quietly exceed the data access, spending limits, or approval gates the original user imposed, turning delegation into a privilege-escalation channel.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, arXiv:2503.18666; Tamarin prover, authorization-protocol modeling facilities.

title: Crash-safe agent action ledgers
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: When an agent crashes and resumes, how can we be sure it will not re-execute or misattribute the actions it already took? The goal is to prove that an agent's retained action state, approvals, retries, and tool outcomes preserve the declared side-effect semantics across crashes and continuation.
status: Crash-safe systems and distributed logics provide suitable foundations — e.g., Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*, and Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove* — but applying them to nondeterministic agent workflows requires an explicit action protocol; recent work such as Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, addresses agent specification but not this crash-safety proof.
solved_when: A verified agent action protocol exists whose retained state (approvals, retries, tool outcomes) is proven to preserve declared side-effect semantics across crashes and continuation.
why: Prevents duplicate or unauthorized actions after interruption — a failure mode that is unacceptable as agents gain real-world side effects.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*; Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*.

title: Formal prompt-injection containment at tool boundaries
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can an LLM agent system be given a machine-checked guarantee that untrusted retrieved text — a webpage, a retrieved document, any tool output — cannot authorize new privileges or add external recipients, without any claim of universal semantic immunity to prompt injection? Formally, the goal is a provable bounded security invariant enforced at tool boundaries, stated over observable authority and actions rather than undefined notions of model obedience.
status: Policy enforcement at tool boundaries supplies a practical route to this goal; the consensus is that guarantees must be stated over observable authority and actions rather than over model obedience. Related work includes information-flow security, specifically untrusted-data noninterference with authority; see Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, arXiv:2503.18666, and Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514.
solved_when: A working agent system carries a proof (or machine-checkable argument) of the bounded containment property: untrusted retrieved text cannot cause escalation of privileges or introduction of external recipients, with the guarantee formulated over observable authority and actions.
why: It converts the vague behavioral goal of "robustness to prompt injection" into enforceable system invariants, giving deployed agents a guarantee that holds even when the underlying model is fully manipulable.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, arXiv:2503.18666; Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Proof-generating agents that cannot alter the task
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: How do we guarantee that an automated verifier or coding agent earns its proof score only on the task it was actually given? Formally, how can a pipeline prevent an agent from raising its measured success rate by weakening specifications, deleting assertions, introducing trusted axioms, or otherwise altering the checked artifact?
status: DafnyPro explicitly uses checks against unauthorized changes; broader cross-tool enforcement remains an open target. Related work includes Banerjee et al. (2026), *DafnyPro*, arXiv:2601.05385, and Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467; the problem connects to preventing benchmark gaming and reward hacking in AI evaluation.
solved_when: A verification pipeline demonstrably detects and rejects any agent attempt to improve its score via weakening specifications, deleting assertions, adding trusted axioms, or modifying the checked artifact, with this enforcement working across tools rather than a single system.
why: Without such enforcement, a "successful proof" is evidence about a modified problem, not the requested program, undermining the trustworthiness of agent-generated formal verification and opening the door to reward hacking.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), *DafnyPro*, arXiv:2601.05385; Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467.

title: Repository-scale verified code generation
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can a system autonomously produce and maintain verified changes across an entire existing repository — with its dependencies, interfaces, concurrency, and realistic build constraints — rather than only isolated self-contained functions?
status: DafnyBench (Loughridge et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.08467) and agentic Dafny systems such as AxDafny (Breen et al., 2026, arXiv:2606.32007) show substantial progress on bounded tasks, but repository-scale maintenance remains a different and unaddressed evaluation target.
solved_when: An agent generates modifications to a real repository that are accepted by its proof checker and build system while preserving interface and dependency correctness across the codebase, at repository scale rather than on bounded single-function tasks.
why: It would connect formal code generation to actual software development practice, where changes must respect surrounding code rather than exist in isolation.
key_works: Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467; Breen et al. (2026), *AxDafny: Agentic Verified Code Generation in Dafny*, arXiv:2606.32007.

title: Verified functional correctness plus practical performance
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can code-generation agents produce programs that both satisfy the original functional specification and meet explicit performance constraints, with checked evidence for each? The goal is an agent that, given a specification together with asymptotic or concrete performance targets, returns code whose correctness is machine-verified and whose performance is measured and confirmed.
status: AxDafny distinguishes proof success from runtime performance, showing that high verification scores alone do not establish efficient implementations (Breen et al. (2026), *AxDafny*, arXiv:2606.32007).
solved_when: An agent generates code meeting the original specification and the stated asymptotic or concrete performance constraints, with verified evidence for correctness and measured evidence for performance.
why: It prevents the failure mode of formally correct but unusably slow generated software — programs that pass verification yet are impractical to run.
key_works: Breen et al. (2026), *AxDafny*, arXiv:2606.32007.

title: Contamination-resistant longitudinal agent-verification benchmarks
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Can we construct versioned agent-verification benchmarks whose future changes are held out, whose specifications are hidden, and whose artifacts carry complete provenance, so that they measure verification ability that endures rather than evaporates?
status: DafnyBench (Loughridge et al. (2024), arXiv:2406.08467) provides an important dataset, but static benchmark success does not measure resistance to contamination or maintenance drift; DafnyPro (Banerjee et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.05385) is also relevant.
solved_when: A versioned benchmark suite exists with held-out future changes, hidden specifications, dependency constraints, and complete artifact provenance, and demonstrably measures durable verification ability resistant to contamination and maintenance drift.
why: Such a benchmark separates genuine verification capability from memorization and benchmark-specific behavior, which current static benchmarks cannot do.
key_works: Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467; Banerjee et al. (2026), *DafnyPro*, arXiv:2601.05385.

title: Verified kernel implementation through executable artifacts
open: Can we bridge the gap between a proved type-checking algorithm and the checker binary that actually runs, so that every step — parsing, serialization, compilation, and runtime — is covered by verification?
status: MetaRocq, Lean4Lean, and verified language implementations address different parts of this chain, but algorithm correctness alone does not discharge all executable assumptions (Sozeau et al. (2020), *Coq Coq Correct!*, DOI:10.1145/3371076; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; CakeML project).
solved_when: A verified chain exists that reaches the executable artifact itself: the proved algorithm is connected through verified compilation, runtime, parsing, and serialization, so that algorithm correctness discharges the assumptions of the checker that is actually executed.
why: It makes proof checking trustworthy at the artifact actually run, rather than only at the level of an idealized algorithm.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), *Coq Coq Correct!*, DOI:10.1145/3371076; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; CakeML project.

title: Cross-assistant proof transfer with explicit logical assumptions
open: Can substantial formal proofs be transferred between proof assistants in a way that records, rather than hides, the differences in axioms, universes, equality, and computation rules — and checks each translation step? The goal is a semantics-preserving translation pipeline whose explicit logical assumptions make the trusted base auditable.
status: Dedukti and related logical-framework work provide important interoperability mechanisms (Assaf et al., *Dedukti: A Logical Framework Based on the λΠ-Calculus Modulo Theory*; Cauderlier and Halmagrand (2015), *Checking Zenon Modulo Proofs in Dedukti*, arXiv:1507.08719), but broad semantics-preserving transfer remains a continuing target.
solved_when: A working transfer mechanism exists that moves substantial proofs across assistants, explicitly records axiom, universe, equality, and computation-rule differences between the systems, and mechanically checks every translation step.
why: It avoids duplicating expensive formal developments across assistants and exposes the hidden assumptions a proof silently relies on.
key_works: Assaf et al., *Dedukti: A Logical Framework Based on the λΠ-Calculus Modulo Theory*; Cauderlier and Halmagrand (2015), *Checking Zenon Modulo Proofs in Dedukti*, arXiv:1507.08719.

title: Safe extensible computation inside proof checking
open: Can a proof assistant perform efficient domain-specific computation — beyond its kernel's native reduction — without enlarging the trusted base with unsound external evaluators or opaque plugins? In other words, how do we get extensible computational reflection while keeping the kernel's trusted boundary small and auditable?
status: Existing routes include reflection, extraction, and certified checking; the open difficulty is preserving extensibility while keeping the trusted boundary small, which remains the current target.
solved_when: A proof-assistant architecture exists that admits domain-specific computation as an extensible mechanism while provably confining trust to a small, clearly delimited kernel, with no trusted external evaluators or opaque plugins.
why: It would make large, computation-heavy formal proofs practical in practice, instead of forcing a choice between feasibility and assurance.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), *Coq Coq Correct!*; Tan et al. (2021), *cake_lpr*; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

bib.title: Safe extensible computation inside proof checking

title: Verified extraction across effects and foreign interfaces
open: Can we prove extraction correct not just for pure programs, but for realistic ones — those using effects, external libraries, and language-specific target representations? A full account would formalize the correctness of extraction even when the extracted code depends on assumptions made by the target runtime.
status: MetaRocq verifies substantial type-checking and erasure foundations (Sozeau et al. 2020, DOI:10.1145/3371076), and extensions of MetaCoq erasure to extraction targeting Rust and Elm (Annenkov, Milo, Nielsen, and Spitters, 2021, *Extending MetaCoq Erasure: Extraction to Rust and Elm*) demonstrate additional directions.
solved_when: A verified extraction procedure exists whose correctness proof covers programs using effects, foreign libraries, and language-specific representations, including the assumptions of the target runtime.
why: It makes the executable programs we actually run inherit the intended meaning of the proofs established at the source level; without it, extraction remains a trusted gap between verified source and running code.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), DOI:10.1145/3371076; Annenkov, Milo, Nielsen, and Spitters (2021), *Extending MetaCoq Erasure: Extraction to Rust and Elm*.

bib.title: Verified extraction across effects and foreign interfaces

title: Adversarially robust proof checking
open: Can a proof checker be made robust against adversarial inputs — maliciously expensive terms, parser attacks, resource exhaustion, and corrupted proof artifacts — while still accepting valid ordinary workloads without excessive false rejections? In other words, can the small trusted computing base of a verifier be hardened so that logical soundness extends to implementation-level security and availability?
status: Small logical kernels address logical soundness, but do not automatically provide implementation security or denial-of-service resistance; existing work includes Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*, and Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*.
solved_when: A proof checker exists that rejects or safely bounds maliciously expensive terms, parser attacks, resource-exhaustion attempts, and corrupted proof artifacts, while demonstrably not rejecting valid ordinary workloads unnecessarily.
why: It would allow proof checking to run as an exposed service or act as a supply-chain gate, where untrusted parties submit proofs and the checker must neither be compromised nor taken down.
key_works: Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*.

bib.title: Adversarially robust proof checking

title: Proof-preserving parallel and distributed kernel checking
open: Can we check the proofs of a large verification project on many machines in parallel, in a way that preserves the guarantees of sequential proof checking? Concretely, this means a verified partitioning of proof dependencies across workers, a deterministic acceptance criterion, and sound recovery when a worker fails.
status: Parallel regression proving exists (e.g., Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2018), *piCoq: Parallel Regression Proving for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*), but foundationally justified distributed checking and operational recovery are stronger requirements that current work does not meet.
solved_when: A distributed kernel-checking implementation exists that (a) partitions the proof dependency graph in a verified manner, (b) accepts if and only if the sequential kernel would accept, deterministically, and (c) recovers soundly from worker failure without re-establishing trust in a centralized scheduler.
why: It would scale proof validation to large projects without centralizing trust in an unchecked scheduler, keeping the trusted base small even as checking is distributed.
key_works: Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2018), *piCoq: Parallel Regression Proving for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*.

bib.title: Proof-preserving parallel and distributed kernel checking

title: Formal assumption accounting for complete developments
open: Can we produce a complete, machine-readable account of everything a delivered formally verified artifact actually relies on — every axiom, admitted theorem, unsafe extension, extraction assumption, and external trust dependency? The goal is an artifact-level, cross-tool report rather than the partial exposures individual proof assistants offer today.
status: Proof assistants already expose portions of this information, but no complete cross-tool, artifact-level account exists. Related efforts include the MetaRocq project documentation, Dedukti framework publications, and Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045; the problem connects to supply-chain security's transitive trust inventories.
solved_when: A delivered artifact is accompanied by a machine-readable report enumerating every axiom, admitted theorem, unsafe extension, extraction assumption, and external trust dependency it uses, complete across proof assistants (a cross-tool account at the artifact level).
why: It turns "formally verified" into a precise, inspectable claim, and gives users the transitive trust inventory needed for supply-chain-style auditing of verified software.
key_works: MetaRocq project documentation; Dedukti framework publications; Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045.

title: Proof repair across semantic data-representation changes
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: When a verified development changes how its data is represented — not merely surface syntax but the underlying structure — can we automatically repair the existing proofs so that the theorems still mean what they originally meant, mediated by an explicit equivalence or refinement map between the old and new representations?
status: Proof-reuse techniques based on ornaments demonstrate meaningful automation for repairing proofs across representation changes, as shown by Ringer, Yazdani, Leo, and Grossman (2019), *Ornaments for Proof Reuse in Coq*, and the same authors (2018), *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*; however, large heterogeneous developments remain challenging.
solved_when: A tool exists that, given a proof development and a semantics-preserving representation change together with an explicit equivalence or refinement map, automatically repairs the proofs so the theorems' meaning is preserved across the change, and this scales beyond small examples to large heterogeneous developments.
why: Without it, verified software is effectively frozen at its original data representations: any substantive restructuring of the underlying data invalidates the proof effort, so verified code cannot evolve the way ordinary software does.
key_works: Ringer, Yazdani, Leo, and Grossman (2019), *Ornaments for Proof Reuse in Coq*; the same authors (2018), *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*.

bib.title: Proof repair across semantic data-representation changes

title: Reliable proof migration between assistant versions
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can we automatically migrate verified developments across changes in libraries, elaboration, tactics, and kernel interfaces while ensuring that theorem statements retain their intended meaning?
status: Proof brittleness and maintenance are documented (Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, arXiv:2003.06458, DOI:10.1561/2500000045); however, successful recompilation alone does not establish semantic equivalence of revised statements, so no such migration guarantee currently exists.
solved_when: A tool exists that performs migration automatically and verifies that the semantics of each theorem statement are preserved under the revision, beyond mere successful recompilation.
why: It prevents verified developments from becoming frozen on obsolete toolchains, keeping long-term formalization viable.

title: Semantic dependency tracking for proof reuse
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can a proof assistant track semantic dependencies finely enough that, after an edit to a formal development, exactly the affected proofs are rechecked — no more, no less?
status: iCoq, piCoq, and machine-checked change-impact analysis establish important baselines: Celik, Palmskog, and Gligoric (2017), *iCoq: Regression Proof Selection for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.
solved_when: A dependency-tracking mechanism reuses proofs safely after changes while avoiding rechecking of unrelated developments, demonstrated at the scale of large verification projects.
why: It cuts verification latency in large proof developments, making incremental proof-checking practical the way precise semantic cache invalidation does for build systems.
key_works: Celik, Palmskog, and Gligoric (2017), *iCoq: Regression Proof Selection for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Searchable proof libraries across incompatible vocabularies
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can a search system find, across proof libraries that formalize the same mathematics in incompatible vocabularies and representations, the lemmas a user needs and adapt them for reuse? Formally, the goal is representation-aware retrieval and adaptation of lemmas whose statements are equivalent but whose encodings and naming conventions differ.
status: Learning-based naming, retrieval, and theorem-proving systems provide partial progress, but representation-aware reuse remains harder than text similarity. Key works include Nie et al. (2020), *Deep Generation of Coq Lemma Names Using Elaborated Terms*, and Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover*, arXiv:2505.20613.
solved_when: A user can retrieve relevant lemmas from a library with a different vocabulary and obtain them adapted to the target library's representation, with the system clearly outperforming pure text-similarity search; no further quantitative targets are stated in the record.
why: It would cut down the rediscovery and duplicated formalization that currently plague cross-library proof development.
key_works: Nie et al. (2020), *Deep Generation of Coq Lemma Names Using Elaborated Terms*; Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover*, arXiv:2505.20613.

title: Automated theorem proving beyond familiar benchmark distributions
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can learned theorem provers discover correct proofs when placed outside the distribution they were trained on — in genuinely new theories, unfamiliar libraries, and problems requiring long dependency chains? Concretely, can such a system produce kernel-checked proofs in these unfamiliar settings with success rates that approach its performance on standard benchmarks?
status: Modern learned provers, such as Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover* (arXiv:2505.20613), and DeepSeek-AI (2025), *DeepSeek-Prover-V2*, achieve substantial benchmark progress; however, generalization beyond familiar theorem distributions remains a distinct research problem.
solved_when: A learned prover demonstrates robust proof discovery on genuinely new theories, unfamiliar libraries, and long dependency chains, with all produced proofs verified by a proof kernel.
why: This determines whether learned proving can actually support new verification projects, rather than only improving scores on the benchmark distributions it was trained on.
key_works: Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover*, arXiv:2505.20613; DeepSeek-AI (2025), *DeepSeek-Prover-V2*, project and research resources.

title: Proof minimization without destroying maintainability
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can we automatically optimize generated proofs so that they remain maintainable, not merely small or fast to check?
status: Proof engineering work (Ringer et al., 2019, *QED at Large*; Ringer et al., 2018, *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*) identifies these as competing concerns: the shortest term or fastest current tactic script need not be the easiest proof to maintain. solved_when: A method exists that jointly optimizes generated proofs for checking cost, size, readability, and resistance to future library changes, demonstrated experimentally.
why: Without it, automated proving risks producing an unmanageable maintenance burden that offsets the labor it saves.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*; Ringer et al. (2018), *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*.

subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Can we cut the human effort required to maintain realistically sized verified software by a factor of ten, holding specifications, supported behavior, and trust assumptions fixed?

solved_when: Total human effort across realistic verified-software maintenance tasks is reduced by at least 10× with specifications, supported behavior, and trust assumptions unchanged, measured longitudinally rather than by annotation counts or isolated theorem successes.
why: It would make formal verification economically sustainable for ordinary development, rather than a niche reserved for high-assurance projects.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*; Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Scalable verification of hybrid quantum-classical programs
open: Can we build automated verification tools that handle substantial hybrid quantum-classical programs — combining quantum operations, classical control flow, arrays, loops, and measurement-dependent behavior — rather than only small isolated circuits?
status: Quantum Hoare logics with classical variables already exist, including relative-completeness results (Feng and Ying, 2021, *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*, arXiv:2008.06812, DOI:10.1145/3456877; Ying, 2024, arXiv:2412.09869). Scaling the automation of these logics to real programs is the open target.
solved_when: An automatic verifier exists that proves correctness properties of substantial hybrid programs featuring quantum operations, classical control, arrays, loops, and measurement-dependent behavior.
why: Real quantum software is hybrid, not a bare circuit; scalable verification would let practitioners trust practical quantum algorithm implementations instead of isolated circuit fragments.
key_works: Feng and Ying (2021), *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*, arXiv:2008.06812, DOI:10.1145/3456877; Ying (2024), arXiv:2412.09869.

title: Verified quantum optimization under realistic hardware constraints
open: Can we build a verified quantum compiler that preserves algorithm meaning through optimization and hardware mapping under realistic constraints — connectivity, native gate sets, ancilla management, and measurement-driven adaptive control?
status: VOQC already provides verified circuit optimization (Hietala et al. (2021), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, DOI:10.1145/3434318; extended TOPLAS version (2023)). Broader hardware-aware adaptive compilation remains an extension target.
solved_when: A formally verified optimizer and hardware mapper exists whose correctness proofs cover circuit optimization together with connectivity-constrained mapping, native-gate translation, ancilla management, and measurement-driven control.
why: It preserves algorithm meaning through aggressive quantum compilation, so optimized circuits can be trusted without re-verification of the compiled output.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2021), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, DOI:10.1145/3434318; extended TOPLAS version (2023).

title: Certified approximation budgets for quantum transformations
open: Can we build a verification framework in which the approximation errors introduced at each stage of quantum-circuit manipulation — gate synthesis, circuit rewriting, and finite-precision numerical representation — compose into a single certified bound on the end-to-end behavior of the transformed circuit? Formally, this asks for a quantitative semantics under which each approximate transformation carries a checkable error certificate and these errors compose soundly across the compilation pipeline.
status: Exact circuit verification and verified optimizers provide a foundation, notably Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, and Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic (2017), *QWIRE* (DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009894); however, approximate transformations remain out of reach because they require quantitative semantics that current frameworks lack. Compositional channel-distance bounds from quantum information are a related starting point.
solved_when: A framework exists in which approximate transformations of quantum circuits come with verified, composable error certificates, so that applying gate synthesis, rewriting, and numerical approximation yields a machine-checked bound on the total deviation of the output circuit's behavior from the input's.
why: It would let optimizer designers use genuinely useful approximate optimizations — not just semantics-preserving ones — while still having a certified account of the total error accumulated, preventing silently invalid circuits.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*; Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic (2017), *QWIRE*, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009894.

title: Noise-model-aware quantum correctness
open: Can we verify correctness claims about a noisy quantum implementation under an explicitly modeled noise channel, in a way that cleanly separates what is proved from what is experimentally estimated about the noise?
status: Quantum-program logics establish semantic foundations — see Ying (2012), *Floyd–Hoare Logic for Quantum Programs*, DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708, and Feng and Ying (2021), DOI:10.1145/3456877 — but operational noise characterization must be connected to these logics rather than presumed; validated noise models under drift remain a separate line of work.
solved_when: A verification framework exists that takes an explicit channel model as input, produces formal guarantees relative to that model, and distinguishes proved consequences from noise parameters that are experimentally estimated rather than assumed.
why: It would make formal guarantees meaningful for imperfect hardware, where noise is the rule rather than the exception.
key_works: Ying (2012), *Floyd–Hoare Logic for Quantum Programs*, DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708; Feng and Ying (2021), DOI:10.1145/3456877.

title: Verified quantum error-correction controllers
open: Can we build a complete quantum error-correction controller — syndrome processing, decoding interfaces, feed-forward control, and fault handling — with a machine-checked correctness proof under an explicitly stated fault model?
status: Existing work supplies pieces but not the whole: quantum circuit verification and hybrid quantum-classical verification provide components (Feng and Ying, 2021, *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*; Hietala et al., 2023, *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*), while complete operational error-correction stacks still carry unmet classical timing and reliability obligations.
solved_when: Every layer of the controller (syndrome processing, decoding interfaces, feed-forward control, and fault handling) is verified against an explicit fault model, yielding a complete operational error-correction stack whose classical timing and reliability obligations are discharged.
why: It establishes fault tolerance for quantum computation as a verified system rather than a collection of separately trusted parts, so the classical control loop can no longer be a silent source of failure.
key_works: Feng and Ying (2021), *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*; Hietala et al. (2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*.

title: Automated quantum loop invariants
open: Can we automatically discover compact, checkable invariants for quantum while-loops? A sharper formulation asks for methods that find and verify such invariants without ever expanding the exponentially large state matrices of the quantum system, whenever the loop's structure permits a compressed representation.
status: Quantum Hoare logic is established as the foundational framework (Ying, 2012, DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708), but automation has lagged; 2025 work (*Automating Quantum Hoare Logic with Automata*, Workshop on Quantum Software) investigates automata-based automation specifically to address the representation and scaling bottlenecks.
solved_when: An automated technique exists that both synthesizes loop invariants for quantum programs and checks them, with complexity that avoids explicit expansion of the exponentially large state representation whenever the program's structure allows — demonstrating improved representation and scaling over direct matrix-based Hoare-logic reasoning.
why: It turns verification of iterative quantum algorithms from a hand-proved, exponentially costly chore into a practical automated routine, which is essential as quantum programs with loops become widespread.
key_works: *Automating Quantum Hoare Logic with Automata* (2025), Workshop on Quantum Software; Ying (2012), DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708.

title: Verified quantum-language interoperability
open: Can we prove that translations among quantum circuit languages, hybrid programming languages, and hardware execution formats preserve program semantics — including measurement behavior and classical state? A full solution would give a formal, machine-checked account of cross-language translation rather than verified pieces within a single tool.
status: QWIRE (Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic, 2017) and verified quantum compilers such as Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, supply important local foundations; cross-tool semantic alignment remains a broader target.
solved_when: A semantics-preserving translation exists, with proof, between circuit languages, hybrid quantum programming languages, and hardware execution formats, and the account explicitly covers measurement and classical state.
why: It closes correctness gaps that arise when independently developed quantum tools are composed — programs moving between tools could currently change meaning without anyone noticing.
key_works: Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic (2017), *QWIRE*; Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*.

title: Quantum-verification benchmarks with known proof obligations
open: Can the quantum-verification community be given a shared benchmark corpus of realistic quantum programs, their transformations, and seeded faults, each paired with expected properties whose verification obligations are stated explicitly and independently checked?
status: Quantum verification frameworks such as the QWIRE project and the VOQC project (including its extended optimizer paper) publish examples and artifacts, and Liu et al. (2019), *Formal Verification of Quantum Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-25543-5_12, verify specific algorithms; but no shared, longitudinal benchmark with explicit semantic and noise assumptions yet exists.
solved_when: A versioned, longitudinal benchmark corpus exists containing realistic quantum programs, transformations, and seeded faults with independently checked expected properties, together with explicit semantic and noise assumptions.
why: It makes progress comparable across proof approaches, replacing scattered per-framework examples with reproducible correctness evaluation.
key_works: QWIRE project publications; VOQC project and extended optimizer paper; Liu et al. (2019), *Formal Verification of Quantum Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-25543-5_12.

title: Smart-contract proofs preserved across upgrades
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can we formally verify that a smart contract upgrade preserves the properties the contract was originally proven to satisfy — even when the upgrade changes storage layouts, reconfigures authorization, can be rolled back, and must interoperate with clients running the old version?
status: ConCert and deployed contract-verification tools establish substantial foundations for smart-contract verification in Coq (Annenkov, Nielsen, and Spitters, 2020, arXiv:1907.10674; arXiv:2201.04919), but upgrade-lifecycle correctness — proof preservation across upgrades — remains a distinct, unaddressed target.
solved_when: A verification framework exists that proves preservation of designated invariants across an upgrade lifecycle, covering storage-layout migration, authorization changes, rollback, and mixed-version (old/new) interactions.
why: Smart contracts hold persistent assets and state that cannot simply be restored if an upgrade silently breaks an invariant; verified upgrade preservation is what makes safe software evolution possible on immutable-state systems.
key_works: Annenkov, Nielsen, and Spitters (2020), *ConCert: A Smart Contract Certification Framework in Coq*, arXiv:1907.10674; *Translation Certification for Smart Contracts* (2022), arXiv:2201.04919.

title: Cross-contract compositional economic invariants
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can we verify that a system of interacting smart contracts jointly preserves conservation, solvency, and access invariants, given explicit assumptions about external protocols and price inputs — even when each contract is individually correct?
status: Individual-contract functional verification is available (e.g., ConCert by Annenkov et al. (2020), arXiv:1907.10674; KEVM, *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine*, 2018), but it does not establish arbitrary compositional or economic safety across interacting contracts.
solved_when: A verification method or tool exists that establishes system-wide conservation, solvency, and access invariants across interacting contracts under explicit assumptions about external protocols and price inputs, going beyond single-contract functional verification.
why: It targets failures that emerge from the interaction of contracts rather than local coding mistakes, which is precisely where compositional and economic safety currently breaks down.
key_works: Annenkov et al. (2020), *ConCert*, arXiv:1907.10674; KEVM, *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine* (2018).

title: Contract guarantees under transaction reordering and censorship
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can we prove properties of smart-contract applications when an adversary controls the order in which transactions are included, delays them, or censors them outright? That is, can application-level guarantees be established under an explicitly modeled adversarial transaction scheduler with bounded or unbounded censorship?
status: Executable blockchain semantics (e.g., KEVM, 2018, *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine*; ConCert, arXiv:1907.10674) support operational reasoning, but economic and liveness claims require an explicit transaction-scheduling model, which is not yet incorporated. Related techniques exist in distributed computing (adversarial scheduling) and mechanism design (transaction-ordering incentives).
solved_when: A verification framework exists in which contract properties are proved sound under an explicit model of adversarial ordering, delayed inclusion, and censorship (whether bounded or unbounded), rather than assuming a favorable or fixed transaction order.
why: Without such a model, local proofs silently assume benign ordering, so contracts verified "correct" can still fail economically or lose liveness when reordered or censored in deployment.
key_works: KEVM (2018), *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine*; ConCert, arXiv:1907.10674.

title: Verified cross-chain bridge implementations
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can we build a cross-chain bridge whose entire execution path — from source-chain finality assumptions through message authentication, replay protection, and validator-set changes, down to destination-chain execution — is formally verified end to end?
status: The building blocks exist: contract-semantics efforts such as KEVM, verification frameworks like ConCert, and security-protocol tools such as the Tamarin prover. No bridge theorem yet composes these into a result that exposes the assumptions of both chains and any external signers.
solved_when: A machine-checked theorem covers the complete bridge path, including source finality assumptions, message authentication, replay protection, validator changes, and destination execution, and explicitly exposes the assumptions of both chains and any external signers.
why: Bridge failures concentrate at trust boundaries between independently governed ledgers, so an end-to-end theorem is what actually pins down where the security argument rests.
key_works: KEVM project; ConCert; Tamarin prover documentation.

title: Verified WebAssembly host and component boundaries
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: How do we extend formal verification from the WebAssembly core language to everything around it — host imports, resource handles, callbacks, and component-level linking — so that security and functional contracts hold across the whole boundary? Concretely, can we prove the contracts of a Wasm module together with the host APIs and components it interacts with, rather than each in isolation?
status: WasmCert provides type-safety and interpreter-related results, including the WasmCert-Rocq and WasmCert-Isabelle projects and Iris-Wasm-related program-logic resources linked by WasmCert. However, core-language soundness does not automatically verify arbitrary host APIs.
solved_when: A verification framework exists that proves security and functional contracts spanning WebAssembly modules, host imports, resource handles, callbacks, and component-level linking — not just core-language soundness but arbitrary host APIs.
why: Without it, sandbox guarantees proven for the core language say nothing about the host APIs real applications actually call, so the guarantees are hollow in practice; with it, they become meaningful for deployed multi-language applications.
key_works: WasmCert-Rocq and WasmCert-Isabelle projects; Iris-Wasm-related program-logic resources linked by WasmCert.

title: Cross-layer verification of API serialization
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can we prove end-to-end agreement of a serialization API across all its layers — so that schemas, parsers, serializers, client types, and server handlers provably agree on values, error behavior, optional fields, and version compatibility? In formal terms, this asks for a single verified specification linking every independently generated artifact in the API's toolchain.
status: Verified query and language frameworks provide relevant techniques, but API contracts frequently span several independently generated artifacts, and no end-to-end cross-layer guarantee is currently available. Key works include Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL* (HAL:hal-02422532) and Auerbach et al. (2017), *Q*cert*.
solved_when: A verifiable artifact (or connected chain of artifacts) demonstrates that schema, parser, serializer, client types, and server handlers agree on values, errors, optional-field handling, and version compatibility.
why: Without it, semantic mismatches slip through component-local type checking, causing runtime failures between layers that each looked correct in isolation.
key_works: Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL*, HAL:hal-02422532; Auerbach et al. (2017), *Q*cert*.

title: Verified application behavior across client, server, and database
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Can a realistic web application's user-visible behavior — every click, query, and committed transaction — be tied by a single verified refinement to its client code, server logic, and database operations, even under retries and partial failure?
status: GraphQL formalization, query verification, and distributed-system proofs each cover portions of the problem; the integrated application-level guarantee remains the target. Key works include Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*; and Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.
solved_when: An end-to-end refinement is established from user-visible operations down to client code, service logic, and persistent transactions, with retries and partial failure handled.
why: It makes formal assurance apply to the behavior users actually observe, rather than to each layer in isolation.
key_works: Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Causal measurement of formal verification’s defect-reduction effect
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Does formal verification causally reduce defects relative to matched conventional development, and by how much? This calls for preregistered, adequately powered studies comparing matched development approaches while measuring escaped defects, severity, labor, and maintenance.
status: Industrial deployments and surveys demonstrate feasibility and report benefits, but they do not by themselves identify a general causal effect; see Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652, and Newcombe et al. (2015), DOI:10.1145/2699417.
solved_when: A preregistered, adequately powered study of matched development approaches exists that measures escaped defects, severity, labor, and maintenance, and supports (or refutes) a general causal effect of formal verification on defect reduction.
why: Without causal evidence, we cannot tell whether observed benefits come from verification itself or from confounding factors; a credible answer would guide where verification produces the greatest practical value.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652; Newcombe et al. (2015), DOI:10.1145/2699417.
