title: Longitudinal total-cost dataset for verified software
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Can we build a longitudinal dataset that tracks the total cost of verified software across its entire life — not just the initial proof, but specification work, proof construction, onboarding, tool migration, defect repair, and ongoing maintenance, all recorded under a comparable accounting scheme?
status: Case studies and surveys contain valuable observations, but no existing dataset captures full lifecycle costs rather than initial proof effort alone; the proposed dataset must close that gap. Related work includes Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652, and Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.
solved_when: A multi-year dataset exists covering specification work, proof construction, onboarding, tool migration, defect repair, and operational maintenance for verified software projects, with accounting methods comparable across records.
why: It enables realistic budgeting and meaningful comparison of verification approaches; without full lifecycle cost data, evaluations rest on initial proof effort alone and systematically misestimate what verification costs.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Dataset of failures outside formal proof boundaries
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Can we build a curated, adjudicated corpus of real-world incidents in which formally verified components were implicated, with each failure classified by whether it stemmed from the specification, the assumptions, the integration, the deployment, or the proof tooling itself? Such a dataset would tell us where verification actually stops protecting us.
status: Existing deployed-system reviews — including the seL4 verification assumptions documentation and Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652 — identify assurance boundaries of verified systems, but no structured incident corpus yet exists to support more precise risk analysis.
solved_when: A publicly documented corpus of incidents exists in which verified components were involved, each incident adjudicated and classified as arising from specifications, assumptions, integration, deployment, or proof-tool defects.
why: It reveals where additional verification would actually prevent failures, allowing verification effort and risk analysis to target the true sources of defects rather than assumed ones.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652; seL4 verification assumptions documentation.

title: Cross-tool semantic benchmark registry
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Can the community build a shared registry that gives every verification benchmark a stable identity, recording its exact semantics, version, expected results, certificates, licensing, and known reductions between equivalent instances?
status: SYNTCOMP, VNN-COMP, DafnyBench (Loughridge et al., 2024), and JANI (Budde et al., 2017) provide important domain-specific infrastructure; the goal is interoperability with these projects, not replacing them.
solved_when: A registry exists that maintains, for each registered benchmark, its identity, exact semantics, versions, expected results, certificates, licensing, and documented reductions between equivalent instances.
why: It prevents misleading tool comparisons that arise when benchmarks carry different semantics or have been silently modified between evaluations.
key_works: SYNTCOMP; VNN-COMP; Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*; Budde et al. (2017), *JANI: Quantitative Model and Tool Interaction*.

title: Reusable assurance evidence across procurement and certification
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: How can assurance evidence—once independently checked—be reused across organizations and certification regimes without either hiding the assumptions it rests on or forcing each recipient to redo the verification from scratch? The goal is to develop evidence formats and acceptance processes that make such reuse both transparent and economical.
status: Verified software already reaches real deployments, and CompCert has documented certification-related adoption; the remaining target is economical, transparent evidence reuse rather than initial regulatory acceptance. Related work includes the CompCert project (2026 qualification and deployment news), Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627, and Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652, on portable technical assurance evidence in standards and procurement.
solved_when: Evidence formats and acceptance processes exist that let independently checked proofs be transferred across organizations without concealment of assumptions and without requiring complete redevelopment by the receiving party.
why: It would eliminate duplicated assurance work when verified components cross organizational boundaries and create economic reward for building and maintaining reusable verified components.
key_works: CompCert project, 2026 qualification and deployment news; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Independent replication infrastructure for formal-methods claims
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Can the formal-methods community build and sustain an infrastructure that independently replicates published claims — proofs, solver results, reported speedups, and toolchain assumptions — rather than checking them once at publication time? Such a system would combine archived environments with independently maintained checkers so that any machine-checked claim can be re-verified on demand, by parties other than its authors.
status: Artifact evaluation, competitions, and verified checkers currently supply the components needed for such a system — e.g. Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*; and VNN-COMP and SYNTCOMP resources — but continuous independent replication across the field remains a proposed infrastructure target rather than an operating reality.
solved_when: Published proofs, solver results, claimed speedups, and toolchain assumptions can be re-checked repeatably using archived environments and independently maintained checkers, with the funding and operation of this replication infrastructure sustained continuously across the field.
why: Without it, "machine checked" risks becoming a claim that cannot be reproduced after publication, eroding the core epistemic guarantee of formal methods; with it, verified claims remain checkable by anyone at any time.
key_works: Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*; VNN-COMP and SYNTCOMP resources.
